   333	\begin{lemma}[Composition over time blocks and regularized products]
   334	  \label{L:raw-block-restart}
   335	  Fix $\delta,B,N$ and let $L = \delta^{-1}$, $L_{\mathrm{ext}} = (N+1)B \ge L$.
   336	  On this global fast horizon define $A_{\mathrm{glob}} = g_\delta
   337	  A_R(W_{\mathrm{fast}})$. Its physical flow obeys
   338	  \begin{equation}\label{E:raw-block-restart}
   339	    P_{\mathrm{glob}}(mB+u,mB)=D_m^0(u),\qquad 0\le u\le B.
   340	  \end{equation}
   341	  The analogous identity holds with the deterministic mean $V_{\delta t}$ added
   342	  globally and local operator paths $X_m+H_m$. Their finite block products,
   343	  including the last remainder $\tau$, are source limits in $L^2$, at this fixed
   344	  $\delta,N$.
   345	\end{lemma}
   346	
   347	\begin{proof}
   348	  Take one regularized slow noise preserving the given noise $Y_{\epsilon,\eta}$
   349	  on the extension of the given $W$ constructed in
   350	  Section~\ref{S:source-driver-convergence}. Define the fast and local noises by
   351	  \[
   352	    Y_{\mathrm{fast}}(f)=Y_{\epsilon,\eta}(T_{\delta,0}f),\qquad
   353	    Y_m(f)=Y_{\epsilon,\eta}(T_{\delta,m}f).
   354	  \]
   355	  The pullback isometry and~\eqref{E:source-two-dominations} give source and
   356	  residual variance bounds by $\|f\|_{H_W}^2$. The residual tends to zero on
   357	  each transformed smooth compact test at fixed $\delta,m$. Joint Gaussianity is
   358	  retained. Proposition~\ref{P:source-gaussian-transfer} therefore gives the
   359	  $L^pC^\theta$ operator-path limits on $[0,L_{\mathrm{ext}}]$ and on $[0,B]$,
   360	  including both constant columns.
   361	
   362	  Their random fields are $Y_{\mathrm{fast}}(u,x) =
   363	  \delta^{a/2}Y_{\epsilon,\eta}(\delta u,x)$ and $Y_m(u,x) =
   364	  Y_{\mathrm{fast}}(mB+u,x)$. Indeed, these follow by change of variables in
   365	  their test integrals. The temporal law is $K_{\eta/\delta}$ because
   366	  $\delta^aK_\eta(\delta r) = K_{\eta/\delta}(r)$; the spatial heat law and all
   367	  joint width rules are unchanged. They are continuous in time and smooth in
   368	  space. Their ordinary primitives equal their Gaussian operator paths: their
   369	  matrix entries are $Y_m(h_R)$, by the indicator approximation used
   370	  in~\eqref{E:raw-block-mean-jacobian} and the point-test integral identity.
   371	  Total finite propagation extends this identity to both constant columns. This
   372	  does not assume a separately chosen extension preserving the given noise
   373	  automatically commutes with time dilation.
   374	
   375	  Changing the ordinary source integration variable and composing the free
   376	  groups gives the exact identity on $F$
   377	  \[
   378	    S_F(mB)\big[A_{\mathrm{glob}}^{\mathrm{src}}(mB+u)
   379	    -A_{\mathrm{glob}}^{\mathrm{src}}(mB)\big]
   380	    S_F(-mB)=X_m^{\mathrm{src}}(u).
   381	  \]
   382	  No physical mask is commuted through a wave group. Restriction, difference and
   383	  conjugation are bounded maps on these fixed-horizon $C^\theta$ spaces. Passing
   384	  the source limits gives the same identity for $A_{\mathrm{glob}},X_m$. For the
   385	  finitely many $m$, a convergent subsequence or rational times and path
   386	  continuity gives simultaneous identities in $u$. Conjugation norms need only
   387	  be finite at this fixed $\delta$.
   388	
   389	  Conjugate the global interaction Young equation on $[mB,mB+u]$ by $S_F(mB)$.
   390	  Bounded linearity of its Riemann sums and that original identity give the
   391	  local equation driven by $X_m$. Uniqueness identifies it with $U_{X_m}$,
   392	  proving \eqref{E:raw-block-restart}. The ordinary deterministic primitive for
   393	  $V_{\delta t}$ has the identical cocycle with local $H_m$. Composition now
   394	  identifies the full product, with terminal $\tau$.
   395	
   396	  For completeness, source convergence of these finite products requires no
   397	  growing-product stability assertion. At fixed $\delta,N$ let $C \ge 1$ be the
   398	  maximum norm of their source and original factors, and let $e_{\mathrm{src}}$
   399	  be the maximum factor difference. The parent Young convergence gives every
   400	  finite moment of $C$ uniformly in source widths and $e_{\mathrm{src}} \to 0$
   401	  in every finite $L^p$. If $d(n)$ is the difference of the first $n$ ordered
   402	  products, then
   403	  \[
   404	    d(n+1)\le C d(n)+C^n e_{\mathrm{src}},\qquad d(0)=0.
   405	  \]
   406	  Extend both finite sequences by identities so the recurrence holds for all
   407	  natural $n$. The finite error-accumulation estimate gives $d(N+1) \le
   408	  (N+1)C^{N+1}e_{\mathrm{src}}$. H\"older, using $C$ in $L^{4(N+1)}$ and the
   409	  error in $L^4$, proves $L^2$ convergence. This is only a fixed-$\delta$ source
   410	  limit. Shifted source products may use the fixed original mean plus the
   411	  regularized noise; no finite-source Cameron mean is substituted. This proves
   412	  Lemma~\ref{L:raw-block-restart}.
   413	\end{proof}

    57	
    58	\begin{lemma}[Basis in the prescribed quotient]\label{L:driver-noise-basis}
    59	  The nonzero space $H_W$ is separable and infinite-dimensional. It has a real
    60	  orthonormal basis with compact smooth representatives, whose evaluations by
    61	  $W$ are independent standard real Gaussians.
    62	\end{lemma}
    63	
    64	\begin{proof}
    65	  For tests supported in $[0,L]\times K$, with $K$ compact, the physical
    66	  covariance and the temporal Schur bound give the absolute estimate
    67	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-test-continuity}
    68	    |\langle F,G\rangle_{H_W}|
    69	    \le |K|\Gamma(K-K)\frac{2L^{1-a}}{1-a}
    70	    \|\|F(t)\|_\infty\|_{L^2(0,L)}
    71	    \|\|G(t)\|_\infty\|_{L^2(0,L)}.
    72	  \end{equation}
    73	  Only spatial differences in $K-K$ contribute. On each rational compact box
    74	  inside positive time, rational step approximations followed by compact smooth
    75	  mollifiers at rational scales give a countable uniformly dense test
    76	  collection, supported in a fixed slightly larger box. The estimate proves
    77	  noise-norm approximation. The union over increasing boxes is dense in the test
    78	  completion. This proves separability without assuming the covariance form is
    79	  injective.
    80	
    81	  Choose $L \ge 1$ with $0 < \Gamma(B_L) < \infty$ and nonnegative compact
    82	  smooth $q \ge 1$ on $B_{2L+1}$. Then
    83	  \[
    84	    Q_{\rm sp}:=\int\Gamma(\ud y)\int q(x)q(x-y)\ud x
    85	    \ge |B_{L+1}|\Gamma(B_L)>0,
    86	  \]
    87	  and the compact-support estimate makes it finite. For every real compact
    88	  smooth positive-time $\tau$, the tensor identity is
    89	  \[
    90	    \|\tau\otimes q\|_{H_W}^2=Q_{\rm sp}\|\tau\|_a^2.
    91	  \]
    92	  Here the temporal norm is computed on any finite interval containing the
    93	  support of $\tau$. It is strictly positive for signed nonzero $\tau$. Indeed,
    94	  zero-extend this deterministic test and use the positive Laplace factorization
    95	  from Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion} to write
    96	  \begin{align*}
    97	    \|\tau\|_a^2
    98	    &=\frac1{\Gamma_E(a)}\int_0^\infty\lambda^{a-1}
    99	    E_\lambda(\tau)\ud\lambda,\\
   100	    E_\lambda(\tau)
   101	    &=\int_\R 2\lambda\left|\int_r^\infty
   102	    e^{-\lambda(t-r)}\tau(t)\ud t\right|^2\ud r.
   103	  \end{align*}
   104	  Signed exchanges are absolutely integrable on the test support, by the
   105	  temporal Schur estimate. If the norm vanished, some $\lambda > 0$ would have
   106	  $E_\lambda = 0$. Its inner integral $v(r)$ is continuous and satisfies $v' =
   107	  \lambda v-\tau$. Vanishing almost everywhere makes it identically zero and
   108	  forces $\tau = 0$. Thus, infinitely many linearly independent compact time
   109	  bumps inject into $H_W$ after multiplication by $q$.
   110	
   111	  Apply Gram--Schmidt to a countable dense real test collection, discarding zero
   112	  residuals in the given null quotient. Infinitude gives an infinite basis; each
   113	  representative is a finite linear combination of compact smooth tests. The
   114	  isonormal identity gives $\E g_jg_k = \delta_{jk}$. Joint Gaussian
   115	  characteristic functions then factor, giving independence and unit variances.
   116	  No physical null direction is removed beyond the prescribed quotient, and no
   117	  $H_W$-valued white Gaussian vector is used. This proves
   118	  Lemma~\ref{L:driver-noise-basis}.
   119	\end{proof}

   121	\begin{lemma}[Covariance coefficients]\label{L:driver-covariance-coefficients}
   122	  For each basis representative put
   123	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-covariance-coefficient}
   124	    H_{j,R}(t,x)=\zeta_R(x)\int_{u>0}|t-u|^{-a}
   125	    \int\Gamma(\ud y)f_j(u,x-y)\ud u.

126	  \end{equation}
   127	  These functions are real smooth on finite time-space compacts, supported
   128	  spatially in $B_{2R}$, with bounded derivatives there. For smooth compact real
   129	  positive-time $F$, and also for the admitted wave tests
   130	  of~\eqref{E:variance-actual-form},
   131	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-literal-covariance}
   132	    \E[W_{\mathbb{C}}(\zeta_RF)g_j]
   133	    =\int H_{j,R}(t,x)F(t,x)\ud t\ud x.
   134	  \end{equation}

   140	  expression is $\int_\R |v|^{-a}\int\Gamma(\ud y)f_j(t-v,x-y)\ud v$. On each

   142	  compact set of $y$. Local Radon mass and local integrability of $|v|^{-a}$

   144	  integration proves smoothness and the derivative bounds. Multiplication by
   145	  $\zeta_R$ gives the stated support. Zero extension is only of a deterministic
   146	  test; no negative-time noise is introduced.

   148	  The physical covariance formula and absolute Fubini give
   149	  \eqref{E:driver-literal-covariance} first for real compact tests. The compact

   158	  coefficients zero as a distribution for $t > 0$. Smoothness, then continuity

   160	  Lemma~\ref{L:driver-covariance-coefficients}.

   163	\subsection{Gain, adjoints and localization}
   164	
   165	\begin{lemma}[Deterministic coefficient operators]\label{L:driver-gain-localization}
   166	  For $I \subset [0,T]$, the statewise integral
   167	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-coefficient-operator}
   168	    A_j(I)z=\int_I S(-t)B(H_{j,R}(t))S(t)z\ud t
   169	  \end{equation}
   170	  satisfies, for every real $r$,
   171	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-gain-one}
   172	    \|A_j(I)\|_{\mathcal{B}(E_r,E_{r+1})}
   173	    \le C_{j,r,R,T}|I|.
   174	  \end{equation}
   175	  Its $E_s$ adjoint has the gain $E_{2s-r-1} \to E_{2s-r}$, so both operators
   176	  act from $E_{s-\gamma}$ to $E$. Choose real compact smooth $\chi = 1$ on
   177	  $B_{2R+T+1}$. On every $E_r$,
   178	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-actual-localization}
   179	    D_\chi A_j(I)=A_j(I)=A_j(I)D_\chi.
   180	  \end{equation}
   181	  For each fixed Schwartz pair,
   182	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-covariance-row}
   183	    \E[g_j\ell_R(I;z,w)]=\langle A_j(I)z,w\rangle_E.
   184	  \end{equation}
   185	\end{lemma}
   186	
   187	\begin{proof}
   188	  The full massless wave is strongly continuous and bounded on every $E_r$ on
   189	  finite time intervals. Its normalized off-diagonal Fourier entries have sizes
   190	  at most $C_T$ and one, respectively; continuity and domination prove the
   191	  strong assertion. Multiplication by $H_{j,R}(t)$ is bounded on every $H^r$,
   192	  continuously in $t$, by weighted Fourier convolution and its compact smooth
   193	  derivative bounds. Hence, $B(H_{j,R}(t)):E_r \to E_{r+1}$ is bounded: its
   194	  second entry is a multiplier of the displacement in $H^r$. The integrand
   195	  in~\eqref{E:driver-coefficient-operator} is strongly continuous with values in
   196	  $E_{r+1}$ for each input in $E_r$, and uniformly bounded in that operator
   197	  norm. Statewise Bochner integration proves~\eqref{E:driver-gain-one},
   198	  including the Lipschitz operator-norm primitive $A_j(0,t)$. Norm continuity of
   199	  $S(t)$ is not needed.
   200	
   201	  Under the $E_s$ pairing, the dual of $E_r$ is isometrically $E_{2s-r}$,
   202	  directly by the two Bessel weights. Dualizing the bound with a gain of one
   203	  derivative therefore gives the asserted adjoint gain. It agrees on Schwartz
   204	  phases with the bounded $E_s$ adjoint. Since $\gamma < 1$, gain one at every
   205	  index implies the two stated maps from $E_{s-\gamma}$ to $E$.
   206	
   207	  For smooth data the free-wave energy on a shrinking ball has nonpositive
   208	  boundary flux: $v\partial_nu-(v^2+|\nabla u|^2)/2 \le 0$. Vanishing initial
   209	  displacement and velocity give zero velocity and gradient in the cone;
   210	  integration of velocity from the zero displacement gives zero displacement
   211	  there as well. Time reversal gives the backward assertion. Thus, both entries
   212	  of $S(\pm t)$ enlarge supports by at most $|t|$. Density and testing against
   213	  compact smooth functions extend this support assertion to Sobolev phases. In
   214	  particular, for input $(1-D_\chi)z$, approximate $z$ by Schwartz phases and
   215	  retain the factor $1-D_\chi$; the approximants vanish on $B_{2R+T+1}$. Their
   216	  free displacement vanishes on $B_{2R}$ throughout $[0,T]$, and the same is
   217	  true in the distributional limit. They contribute nothing to the integral. Its
   218	  output is supported in $B_{2R+T}$, by the support of $H_{j,R}$ and backward
   219	  finite propagation. Since $\chi = 1$ on a neighborhood of this ball, both
   220	  identities in~\eqref{E:driver-actual-localization} follow. This uses both
   221	  entries, not a scalar restart or a positivity theorem.
   222	
   223	  Finally, apply the physical Sobolev pairing
   224	  \eqref{E:variance-physical-adjoint} and~\eqref{E:driver-literal-covariance} to
   225	  the state integral. They give \eqref{E:driver-covariance-row}.
   226	  In~\eqref{E:driver-covariance-coefficient}, the mask is after convolution;
   227	  replacing it by a mask inside $\Gamma*f_j$ would change this identity. This
   228	  proves Lemma~\ref{L:driver-gain-localization}.
   229	\end{proof}

   231	\subsection{Finite variances and first Wiener chaos tails}
   232	
   233	Put $J_0(u,v) = (\Lambda^{1/2}u,\Lambda^{-1/2}v)$, $H_0 = L^2(\R^d;\R^2)$, $a_j
   234	= J_0A_j(I)J_0^{-1}$ and $P_\chi = J_0D_\chi J_0^{-1}$. The operator $D_\gamma =
   235	\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda^{-\gamma},\Lambda^{-\gamma})$ acts on these physical
   236	coordinates. Its two compact envelopes $B_{\rm out},B_{\rm in}$ are those of
   237	Proposition~\ref{P:compact-two-envelopes}, after complexification when Schatten
   238	norms are used. For $I \subset [0,T]$ with $0 < h = |I| \le 1$, set
   239	\begin{equation}\label{E:driver-short-variance-budget}
   240	  b_I=C_T h^{2-a}B_\alpha(h),
   241	\end{equation}
   242	where $C_T$ is the uniform-in-$R$ constant in
   243	Proposition~\ref{P:wave-two-variances}.
   244	
   245	\begin{lemma}[Both variances and their tails]\label{L:driver-actual-variances}
   246	  For every $N$,
   247	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-two-variances}
   248	    V_{{\rm out},N}:=\sum_{j\le N}a_ja_j^*\le b_ID_\gamma^2,
   249	    \qquad V_{{\rm in},N}:=\sum_{j\le N}a_j^*a_j\le b_ID_\gamma^2.
   250	  \end{equation}
   251	  The finite families satisfy both localizations by $P_\chi$. There are bounded
   252	  positive limits $V_{{\rm out},\infty},V_{{\rm in},\infty}$ with positive tails
   253	  $T_{{\rm out},N},T_{{\rm in},N} \to 0$ strongly, and
   254	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-compact-tail-envelopes}
   255	    T_{{\rm out},N}\le b_IB_{\rm out},\qquad
   256	    T_{{\rm in},N}\le b_IB_{\rm in}.
   257	  \end{equation}
   258	  For each fixed $z \in E_{s-\gamma}$, the real column maps satisfy
   259	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-column-expansions}
   260	    m_{R,I}(z)=\sum_jg_jA_j(I)z,\qquad
   261	    n_{R,I}(z)=\sum_jg_jA_j(I)^{*,E}z
   262	    \quad\text{in }L^2(\Omega;E).
   263	  \end{equation}
   264	\end{lemma}
   265	
   266	\begin{proof}
   267	  By~\eqref{E:driver-covariance-row}, for real Schwartz $z,w$,
   268	  \[
   269	    \langle X_N(I)z,w\rangle_E
   270	    =\sum_{j\le N}g_j\E[g_j\ell_R(I;z,w)]
   271	    =\mathcal{P}_N\ell_R(I;z,w),
   272	  \]
   273	  where $\mathcal{P}_N$ is the orthogonal projection in $L^2(\Omega)$ onto the
   274	  span of $g_1,\ldots,g_N$. In particular,
   275	  \[
   276	    \sum_{j\le N}|\langle A_j(I)z,w\rangle_E|^2
   277	    =\E|\langle X_N(I)z,w\rangle_E|^2
   278	    \le\E|\ell_R(I;z,w)|^2.
   279	  \]
   280	  These are projections onto the noise-test basis, not source regularizations.
   281	  The two variance bounds of Proposition~\ref{P:wave-two-variances}, with the
   282	  mean-square columns of Proposition~\ref{P:wave-square-columns}, apply to these
   283	  same covariance forms and the bound~\eqref{E:driver-short-variance-budget}.
   284	
   285	  Choose a real Schwartz orthonormal basis $\{e_k\}$ of $E$. Fix real Schwartz
   286	  $w$. For every finite phase truncation $K$,
   287	  \[
   288	    \begin{split}
   289	      \sum_{k\le K}\sum_{j\le N}
   290	      |\langle A_j(I)e_k,w\rangle_E|^2
   291	      &=\sum_{k\le K}\E|\langle X_N(I)e_k,w\rangle_E|^2\\
   292	      &\le\sum_{k\le K}\E|\ell_R(I;e_k,w)|^2
   293	      \le b_I\|w\|_{E_{s-\gamma}}^2,
   294	    \end{split}
   295	  \]
   296	  by~\eqref{E:wave-input-variance}. Let $K \to \infty$. Parseval in the phase
   297	  space and nonnegative monotone convergence, with $N$ still finite, give
   298	  \[
   299	    \sum_{j\le N}\|A_j(I)^{*,E}w\|_E^2
   300	    =\E\|X_N(I)^{*,E}w\|_E^2
   301	    \le b_I\|w\|_{E_{s-\gamma}}^2.
   302	  \]
   303	  Conversely, for fixed real Schwartz $z$, use \eqref{E:wave-output-variance}
   304	  with the output basis varying:
   305	  \[
   306	    \begin{split}
   307	      \sum_{k\le K}\sum_{j\le N}
   308	      |\langle A_j(I)z,e_k\rangle_E|^2
   309	      &=\sum_{k\le K}\E|\langle X_N(I)z,e_k\rangle_E|^2\\
   310	      &\le\sum_{k\le K}\E|\ell_R(I;z,e_k)|^2
   311	      \le b_I\|z\|_{E_{s-\gamma}}^2.
   312	    \end{split}
   313	  \]
   314	  The same phase Parseval limit gives
   315	  \[
   316	    \sum_{j\le N}\|A_j(I)z\|_E^2
   317	    =\E\|X_N(I)z\|_E^2
   318	    \le b_I\|z\|_{E_{s-\gamma}}^2.
   319	  \]
   320	  Thus, both directions use their respective Hilbert-Bessel bounds; neither
   321	  follows from retaining only one variance.
   322	
   323	  These inequalities extend at each finite $N$ to the full $E_{s-\gamma}$ input
   324	  space. Indeed, Lemma~\ref{L:driver-gain-localization} gives $A_j:E_{s-\gamma}
   325	  \to E_{s+1-\gamma} \subset E$. Its adjoint gain, at $r = s+\gamma-1$, gives
   326	  the same map for $A_j^{*,E}$. The inclusion holds since $\gamma < 1$.
   327	  Approximate the input by Schwartz phases and pass each of the finitely many
   328	  operator terms to the limit. The resulting constant is still $b_I$,
   329	  independent of $N$; individual $j$-dependent gain constants were not summed.
   330	  Restricting to $E$ and using $\|z\|_{E_{s-\gamma}} = \|D_\gamma J_0z\|_{H_0}$
   331	  gives \eqref{E:driver-two-variances} as two operator quadratic inequalities.
   332	  Both localizations follow from~\eqref{E:driver-actual-localization}. No
   333	  self-adjointness or projection property of $P_\chi$ is assumed.
   334	
   335	  The coordinates of $m_{R,I}(z)$, for Schwartz $z$, are the original covariance
   336	  forms $\ell_R(I;z,e_k)$ and belong to the closed first Wiener chaos $W(H_W)$.
   337	  Their coefficients against $g_j$ are $\langle A_jz,e_k\rangle_E$. Parseval in
   338	  that chaos, followed by Parseval in $E$ and positive Tonelli, gives
   339	  \[
   340	    \sum_j\|A_jz\|_E^2=\E\|m_{R,I}(z)\|_E^2,
   341	    \qquad m_{R,I}(z)=\sum_jg_jA_jz\quad\text{in }L^2(\Omega;E).
   342	  \]
   343	  The same argument for the adjoint column gives the other expansion. Membership
   344	  in this first chaos comes from linear noise tests, not merely Gaussianity. To
   345	  extend to a fixed $E_{s-\gamma}$ input, approximate by Schwartz phases. The
   346	  finite inequalities extend to that space by the gain bounds and have a
   347	  constant uniform in $N$. Apply them to the input difference, then use the
   348	  Schwartz expansion and continuity of $m,n$. This
   349	  proves~\eqref{E:driver-column-expansions} on the full claimed input domain.
   350	
   351	  The convergent positive quadratic sums, restricted to $E$ and transported by
   352	  $J_0$, define the bounded positive operators $V_{\cdot,\infty}$ by
   353	  polarization and Riesz. They retain the bounds $b_ID_\gamma^2$. Their tails
   354	  have quadratic forms tending to zero. Since they are uniformly bounded and
   355	  positive, $\|T_Nv\|^2 \le \|T_N\|\langle T_Nv,v\rangle \to 0$. Passing to the
   356	  limit in the finite localization identities gives
   357	  \[
   358	    V_{{\rm out},\infty}=P_\chi V_{{\rm out},\infty}P_\chi^*,\qquad
   359	    V_{{\rm in},\infty}=P_\chi^*V_{{\rm in},\infty}P_\chi,
   360	  \]
   361	  and the same identities for their tails. Positive congruence applied to $T_N
   362	  \le b_ID_\gamma^2$ proves~\eqref{E:driver-compact-tail-envelopes}.
   363	
   364	  Complexification preserves these statements and constants. The Hilbert norms
   365	  split into real and imaginary squared norms; real operators extend
   366	  isometrically. A real orthonormal basis complexifies to a complex orthonormal
   367	  basis, preserving singular values and multiplicities. The complex column maps
   368	  have the same bounds and sesquilinear row identities. This proves
   369	  Lemma~\ref{L:driver-actual-variances}.
   370	\end{proof}

   372	\begin{lemma}[Compact domination of positive tails]\label{L:driver-dominated-tails}
   373	  If $0 \le T_N \le B$, with positive compact $B \in S_m$, $m \ge 1$, and $T_N
   374	  \to 0$ weakly, then
   375	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-trace-tails}
   376	    \|T_N\|\longrightarrow0,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}T_N^m\longrightarrow0.
   377	  \end{equation}
   378	\end{lemma}
   379	
   380	\begin{proof}
   381	  Choose a finite spectral projection $Q$ of $B$ with $\|(1-Q)B(1-Q)\| <
   382	  \epsilon$. Positive quadratic Cauchy--Schwarz gives, for unit $x$,
   383	  \[
   384	    \langle T_Nx,x\rangle
   385	    \le2\langle T_NQx,Qx\rangle
   386	    +2\langle T_N(1-Q)x,(1-Q)x\rangle
   387	    \le2\|QT_NQ\|+2\epsilon.
   388	  \]
   389	  Weak convergence makes the finite-dimensional matrix $QT_NQ$ converge in norm
   390	  to zero. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves norm convergence.

391	  Lemma~\ref{L:compact-positive-order} gives $\lambda_j(T_N) \le \lambda_j(B)$,
   392	  while each $\lambda_j(T_N) \to 0$ by norm convergence. Dominated summation of
   393	  $\lambda_j(B)^m$ proves the trace limit. No order comparison of the operator
   394	  powers is used. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:driver-dominated-tails}.
   395	\end{proof}

   397	\begin{lemma}[Retained finite Gaussian variance powers]\label{L:driver-gaussian-tail-average}
   398	  Let $Z_\ell$ be finitely many compact operators whose two variances $V_{\rm
   399	  out},V_{\rm in}$ belong to $S_{q/2}$, for an even $q \ge 2$. With independent
   400	  standard real $g_\ell$,
   401	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-retained-gaussian-average}
   402	    \E\left\|\sum_\ell g_\ell Z_\ell\right\|_{S_q}^q
   403	    \le(q-1)^{q/2}\frac{\operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm out}^{q/2}
   404	    +\operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm in}^{q/2}}2.
   405	  \end{equation}
   406	\end{lemma}
   407	
   408	\begin{proof}
   409	  Compress by finite-rank orthogonal $Q_k \to I$ strongly. The compressed output
   410	  variance is at most $Q_kV_{\rm out}Q_k$, since their difference is $\sum_\ell
   411	  Q_kZ_\ell(1-Q_k)Z_\ell^*Q_k \ge 0$; the input inequality is the same with
   412	  adjoints interchanged. Positive-order and compression max-min compare their
   413	  trace powers with the uncompressed ones. Apply
   414	  Proposition~\ref{P:finite-gaussian-matrix} on the finite range, retaining the
   415	  average. For each finite Gaussian coordinate vector, compactness gives
   416	  operator-norm convergence of the compressed sum to the original sum. The
   417	  singular-value norm-Lipschitz argument in the proof of
   418	  Corollary~\ref{C:finite-gaussian-operators}, then Fatou over singular values
   419	  and probability, proves the displayed bound. The extended norm is measurable
   420	  by the same finite-coordinate continuity argument. No infinite Gaussian series
   421	  or $S_q$-Bochner convergence is assumed. This proves
   422	  Lemma~\ref{L:driver-gaussian-tail-average}.
   423	\end{proof}

   427	\begin{lemma}[Fixed-interval operator construction]\label{L:driver-interval-limit}
   428	  For each fixed short interval $I$, $X_N(I)$ converges in every finite
   429	  $L^p(\Omega;\mathcal{B}(E))$ to a compact-valued centered Gaussian operator
   430	  $X_R(I)$ on the original probability space. For every admissible even $q \ge
   431	  2$, $q\gamma > d$,
   432	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-fixed-schatten}

   434	    \le\sqrt{q-1}\sqrt{C_T}\,h^{1-a/2}B_\alpha(h)^{1/2}

   442	  Proposition~\ref{P:localized-finite-variance} and
   443	  Corollary~\ref{C:finite-gaussian-operators}: both localizations, both weighted
   444	  variances and the independent real $g_j$ have been proved in
   445	  Lemma~\ref{L:driver-actual-variances}. Thus, the coefficients are compact, and
   446	  their finite Gaussian sums satisfy~\eqref{E:driver-fixed-schatten}, uniformly

   450	  envelopes in~\eqref{E:driver-compact-tail-envelopes} belong to $S_{q/2}$.
   451	  Lemma~\ref{L:driver-dominated-tails} therefore gives
   452	  \[
   453	    \operatorname{Tr}T_{{\rm out},N}^{q/2}\longrightarrow0,
   454	    \qquad
   455	    \operatorname{Tr}T_{{\rm in},N}^{q/2}\longrightarrow0.
   456	  \]

   465	  \[
   466	    \sup_{M>N}\E\|Y_{N,M}\|_{S_q}^q
   467	    \le(q-1)^{q/2}

   469	    +\operatorname{Tr}T_{{\rm in},N}^{q/2}}2
   470	    \longrightarrow0.
   471	  \]

   473	  eigenvalues, not operator monotonicity of the $q/2$ power. Since $\|Y_{N,M}\|

   477	  All finite sums lie in the separable operator-norm closed real span
   478	  $\mathcal{F}_I$ of the countably many deterministic $A_j(I)$. Choose $N_k$

   480	  2^{-k}$. Their $L^1$ norms are summable. Tonelli therefore shows that the
   481	  pointwise operator-norm differences sum absolutely almost surely. Completeness
   482	  gives a limit in $\mathcal{F}_I$ on the original probability space; assign it
   483	  zero on the exceptional null set. It is strongly measurable as a limit of
   484	  separably valued finite Gaussian sums. Fatou and the Cauchy property give

   486	  noise or probability space has been introduced. Limits constructed at
   487	  different admissible even indices agree by uniqueness of convergence in

   493	  subsequence makes $X_R(I)$ compact valued. Singular-value Fatou applied to the

   501	  For each fixed real Schwartz $z,w$, the scalar rows $\langle
   502	  X_N(I)z,w\rangle_E$ are the orthogonal projections of the completed covariance

   510	  at most one. Their indicator tests add to the long-interval test except at

   522	  a Schatten-valued path or arbitrary-index claim. This proves
   523	  Lemma~\ref{L:driver-interval-limit}.
   524	\end{proof}

   526	\subsection{Time-path convergence and Gaussian norm bounds}
   527	
   528	\begin{lemma}[H\"older path limit]\label{L:driver-holder-limit}
   529	  The finite paths $X_N(t) = X_N((0,t))$ converge in
   530	  $L^p(\Omega;C^\theta([0,T];\mathcal{B}(E)))$ for every finite $p \ge 1$, in a
   531	  separable closed path span on the same probability space. The limit starts at
   532	  zero and has compact values for all times on one path event. For sufficiently
   533	  large even $q_0$, its $C^\theta$ norm has $L^q$ bound $C\sqrt q$, uniformly
   534	  over even $q \ge q_0$ and the basis.
   535	\end{lemma}
   536	
   537	\begin{proof}
   538	  Choose $\theta < \eta < \beta$ and an even $q_0 \ge 2$ with $q_0\gamma > d$
   539	  and $\beta-\eta-1/q_0 > 0$. For $q \ge q_0$, the singular-value sequence gives
   540	  $\|K_\chi\|_{S_q} \le \|K_\chi\|_{S_{q_0}}$: if the latter is nonzero,
   541	  normalize by it, so every singular value is at most one, and sum its $q$th
   542	  powers. The zero case is immediate. Apply the finite Gaussian operator
   543	  estimate with the time-refined variances from
   544	  Proposition~\ref{P:wave-two-variances}. This gives, uniformly in $N$ and even
   545	  $q \ge q_0$,
   546	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-increment-moments}
   547	    \|X_N(t)-X_N(u)\|_{L^q(\mathcal{B}(E))}
   548	    \le C\sqrt q\,|t-u|^\beta,\qquad |t-u|\le1.
   549	  \end{equation}
   550	  The constant includes the fixed $S_{q_0}$ cutoff norm and does not depend on
   551	  $q$. Longer increments are finite sums of unit increments, with constants
   552	  depending on $T$.
   553	
   554	  Let $D_n(F)$ be the maximum of adjacent increments on the grid $kT2^{-n}$, $0
   555	  \le k \le 2^n$. At fine levels $T2^{-n} \le 1$, the elementary bound for a
   556	  finite maximum yields
   557	  \[
   558	    \|D_n(X_N)\|_{L^q}
   559	    \le 2^{n/q}C\sqrt q\,(T2^{-n})^\beta.
   560	  \]
   561	  No independence of these increments is used. The finitely many coarse levels
   562	  are controlled by unit partitions. Minkowski and a geometric sum therefore
   563	  give
   564	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-dyadic-moment-sum}
   565	    \sup_N\left\|\sum_{n\ge0}2^{n\eta}D_n(X_N)\right\|_{L^q}
   566	    \le C_\eta\sqrt q,
   567	  \end{equation}
   568	  since the fine-level ratio is at most $2^{-(\beta-\eta-1/q_0)} < 1$.
   569	
   570	  For a continuous Banach-valued $F$ starting at zero, this weighted dyadic sum
   571	  controls its $C^\eta$ norm. Approximate two times by dyadic points at a scale
   572	  comparable to their separation. The two grid points differ by at most two
   573	  adjacent increments, and each endpoint's finer binary corrections are bounded
   574	  by the tail sum of $D_n$. Multiplying by the separation to the power $-\eta$
   575	  bounds that total by the weighted sum, up to a constant depending on $T,\eta$.
   576	  Continuity identifies the endpoint limits and also controls the supremum norm
   577	  from $F(0) = 0$. The finite paths are Lipschitz by~\eqref{E:driver-gain-one}.
   578	  Thus, \eqref{E:driver-dyadic-moment-sum} gives uniform $L^qC^\eta$ bounds, and
   579	  the triangle inequality gives the same bound for their differences.
   580	
   581	  On a fixed finite time grid, Lemma~\ref{L:driver-interval-limit} gives $L^q$
   582	  convergence of every point value. For continuous $F$,
   583	  \[
   584	    \|F\|_\infty\le\max_k\|F(t_k)\|
   585	    +C(\operatorname{mesh})^\eta\|F\|_{C^\eta}.
   586	  \]
   587	  Apply this to $X_N-X_M$, send $N,M \to \infty$ at a fixed grid, and then send
   588	  the mesh to zero. The uniform $C^\eta$ bound proves sup-norm $L^q$ Cauchy
   589	  convergence. The deterministic interpolation inequality
   590	  \begin{equation}\label{E:driver-holder-interpolation}
   591	    \|F\|_{C^\theta}
   592	    \le C\|F\|_\infty^{1-\theta/\eta}
   593	    \|F\|_{C^\eta}^{\theta/\eta}
   594	  \end{equation}
   595	  follows by bounding each increment by both $2\|F\|_\infty$ and its $C^\eta$
   596	  bound, and splitting at their balancing scale. Its supremum term is controlled
   597	  too. Scalar H\"older in probability proves the $L^qC^\theta$ Cauchy property.
   598	  For any requested finite $p$, choose an even $q \ge \max(p,q_0)$ and use
   599	  Lyapunov.
   600	
   601	  The full H\"older/operator space need not be separable. Nevertheless, every
   602	  finite path lies in the span of the countably many deterministic Lipschitz
   603	  paths $A_j(0,\cdot)$. Their $C^\theta$-closed real span is a separable Banach
   604	  space. In it the same elementary Cauchy/subsequence construction as in
   605	  Lemma~\ref{L:driver-interval-limit} gives a strongly measurable limit $M_R$ on
   606	  the original space. Different $p$ limits agree by uniqueness of convergence in
   607	  probability in the path norm. An almost surely $C^\theta$-convergent
   608	  subsequence converges uniformly in operator norm. Finite paths have compact
   609	  values on short intervals, and on long ones by finite additivity. Therefore,
   610	  the limit has compact values at every time on that single path set. It starts
   611	  at zero. Passing the uniform bounds from~\eqref{E:driver-dyadic-moment-sum}
   612	  through the path convergence proves the asserted $C\sqrt q$ bound. This proves
   613	  Lemma~\ref{L:driver-holder-limit}.
   614	\end{proof}

   616	\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{P:actual-operator-driver}]
   617	  Lemmas~\ref{L:driver-noise-basis}--\ref{L:driver-holder-limit} construct the
   618	  stated finite sums and their path limit, with no new probability space.
   619	  Evaluation at a fixed time agrees with the interval limit by uniqueness in
   620	  probability. Its covariance identity for matrix elements is
   621	  \eqref{E:driver-raw-row}, by Lemma~\ref{L:driver-interval-limit}, including
   622	  the long-interval interpretation. The same additivity identifies each fixed
   623	  increment with $X_R(I)$, proving its stated Schatten moment bound.
   624	
   625	  The finite paths are Gaussian linear combinations of deterministic paths.
   626	  Every continuous linear functional on their closed path span converges in
   627	  $L^2$ to a centered Gaussian; finite linear combinations do as well. Thus,
   628	  $M_R$ is a centered Gaussian path. The four real pair identities give its
   629	  complexified sesquilinear row identity.
   630	
   631	  The construction used only compact smooth representatives, orthonormality and
   632	  completeness, so it applies to any such noise basis. Compare two constructions
   633	  using a fixed countable dense Schwartz phase collection and rational times.
   634	  Both rows equal the same covariance forms. A countable null-set union,
   635	  boundedness of the operators, phase density and path continuity give equality
   636	  at all times on one probability-one set. This proves indistinguishability
   637	  without an assumed common event for uncountably many original evaluations.
   638	
   639	  For $p \ge 1$, choose even $q \ge \max(p,q_0)$ with $q \le p+q_0+2 \le
   640	  (q_0+3)p$. Lemma~\ref{L:driver-holder-limit} and Lyapunov give the first bound

     2	\label{S:wave-variance}

     4	We now apply the covariance and temporal estimates of
     5	Section~\ref{S:masked-covariance} to the full wave phase. We retain

     8	  0 < \gamma < \min\left(\frac12,\frac{2-\alpha}{2}\right).

    10	The interval is nonempty because $\alpha+a < 2$. We use $\langle\xi\rangle =
    11	\sqrt{1+|\xi|^2}$ and set
    12	\begin{equation}\label{E:variance-scale-profile}
    13	  B_\alpha(h) =
    14	  \begin{cases}
    15	    1, & \alpha < 1,\\
    16	    1+\log(1/h), & \alpha = 1,\\
    17	    h^{1-\alpha}, & \alpha > 1,
    18	  \end{cases}

    22	\subsection{A scalar row estimate for a measure}
    23	
    24	Let $\nu$ be a positive Radon measure satisfying
    25	\begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-translated-growth}
    26	  \nu(B(y,r)) \le C r^\alpha,
    27	  \qquad y \in \R^d,\quad r > 0,
    28	\end{equation}
    29	where $C \ge 0$. If the estimate is initially known for open balls, apply it at
    30	radius $r+\epsilon$ and let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ to obtain the closed-ball
    31	estimate. Neither evenness nor a density is assumed here.
    32	Using~\eqref{E:masked-frequency-pair}, define
    33	\begin{align}
    34	  \Phi_h(\xi,\eta)
    35	  &:= \frac{\mathcal{Q}_h(|\xi|,|\eta|)}
    36	  {\langle\xi\rangle\langle\eta\rangle},
    37	  \label{E:frequency-row-kernel}\\
    38	  J_h(\xi)
    39	  &:= \langle\xi\rangle^{2\gamma}
    40	  \int_{\R^d}\Phi_h(\xi,\xi-\lambda)\nu(\ud\lambda).
    41	  \label{E:frequency-row-integral}
    42	\end{align}
    43	These are initially nonnegative extended integrals. In particular, the notation
    44	denotes a pushforward of $\nu$, not integration against an assumed spectral
    45	density.
    46	
    47	\begin{proposition}[Uniform scalar row]\label{P:frequency-row}
    48	  There is a finite $K = K(\alpha,a,\gamma)$, independent of $d,\nu,C,h$ and
    49	  $\xi$, such that
    50	  \begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-row-bound}
    51	    \sup_{\xi\in\R^d}J_h(\xi) \le K C B_\alpha(h),
    52	    \qquad 0 < h \le 1.
    53	  \end{equation}
    54	\end{proposition}
    55	
    56	\begin{proof}
    57	  If $C = 0$, a countable covering by finite balls gives $\nu = 0$, and the
    58	  result is immediate. Suppose $C > 0$. For each $\xi$, let $\nu_\xi$ be the
    59	  pushforward under $\lambda \mapsto \eta = \xi-\lambda$. Then $\nu_\xi(B(0,R))
    60	  \le CR^\alpha$. For $q \ge 1$, put
    61	  \[
    62	    A_\xi(q) = \int_{|\eta|\le5q}\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}
    63	    \nu_\xi(\ud\eta).
    64	  \]
    65	  Choose $N = \lceil\log_2(5q)\rceil$, so $5q \le 2^N < 10q$. Splitting into the
    66	  unit ball and the annuli $2^j < |\eta| \le 2^{j+1}$ gives
    67	  \[
    68	    A_\xi(q) \le C\left(1+2^\alpha
    69	    \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}2^{j(\alpha-1)}\right).
    70	  \]
    71	  The geometric sum is bounded when $\alpha < 1$, is $N$ when $\alpha = 1$, and
    72	  is at most $2^{N(\alpha-1)}/(2^{\alpha-1}-1)$ when $\alpha > 1$. Hence,
    73	  \begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-inverse-bessel}
    74	    A_\xi(q) \le K_\alpha C
    75	    \begin{cases}
    76	      1, & \alpha < 1,\\
    77	      1+\log q, & \alpha = 1,\\
    78	      q^{\alpha-1}, & \alpha > 1,
    79	    \end{cases}
    80	  \end{equation}
    81	  with a constant depending only on $\alpha$.
    82	
    83	  Set $q = \max(1,|\xi|)$ and $\epsilon = 1-2\gamma > 0$. On $|\lambda| \le 4q$
    84	  we have $|\eta| \le 5q$. Both bracket powers in $\mathcal{Q}_h$ are at most
    85	  one, since $a-1 < 0$. The contribution of this region to $J_h(\xi)$ is at most
    86	  \[
    87	    2\langle\xi\rangle^{-\epsilon}A_\xi(q)
    88	    \le 2q^{-\epsilon}A_\xi(q).
    89	  \]
    90	  If $\alpha < 1$, this is uniformly bounded
    91	  by~\eqref{E:frequency-inverse-bessel}. If $\alpha = 1$, the bound follows from
    92	  \[
    93	    e^{-\epsilon u}(1+u) \le 1+\frac1{e\epsilon},
    94	    \qquad u = \log q \ge 0,
    95	  \]
    96	  since $u e^{-\epsilon u}$ has maximum $1/(e\epsilon)$. If $\alpha > 1$, the
    97	  remaining power is $q^{\alpha+2\gamma-2}$, whose exponent is negative
    98	  by~\eqref{E:variance-gamma-range}. Thus, the near contribution is at most a
    99	  constant times $C$ in all three cases.
   100	
   101	  On the far region write $r = |\lambda| > 4q$. Then
   102	  \[
   103	    |\eta| \ge \frac{3r}4,\qquad
   104	    \big||\eta|-|\xi|\big| \ge \frac r2,\qquad
   105	    |\eta|+|\xi| \ge \frac r2.
   106	  \]
   107	  Each oscillatory bracket is at least $\langle hr\rangle/2$, whereas
   108	  $\langle\eta\rangle^{-1} \le 4/(3r)$ and $\langle\xi\rangle^{-\epsilon} \le
   109	  1$. Consequently, the far contribution is at most
   110	  \[
   111	    \frac43\,2^{2-a}\int_{|\lambda|>4q}
   112	    |\lambda|^{-1}\langle h|\lambda|\rangle^{a-1}\nu(\ud\lambda).
   113	  \]
   114	  Enlarge the domain to $|\lambda| > 1$ and split it into dyadic annuli.
   115	  Applying~\eqref{E:frequency-translated-growth} to their masses bounds this
   116	  expression by a constant depending only on $\alpha,a$ times $C S(h)$, where
   117	  \[
   118	    S(h) = \sum_{j=0}^\infty
   119	    2^{j(\alpha-1)}\langle h2^j\rangle^{a-1}.
   120	  \]
   121	  Choose $L = \lfloor\log_2(1/h)\rfloor \ge 0$. For $j \le L$ the bracket power
   122	  is at most one. For $j \ge L+1$ it is at most $(h2^j)^{a-1}$. Since
   123	  $\alpha+a-2 < 0$, the tail is
   124	  \[
   125	    \frac{h^{a-1}2^{(L+1)(\alpha+a-2)}}{1-2^{\alpha+a-2}}
   126	    \le \frac{h^{1-\alpha}}{1-2^{\alpha+a-2}}.
   127	  \]
   128	  The inequality uses $2^{L+1} > 1/h$ and the negative exponent. The finite sum
   129	  is bounded by $1/(1-2^{\alpha-1})$ for $\alpha < 1$, by $1+\log_2(1/h)$ for
   130	  $\alpha = 1$, and by
   131	  \[
   132	    \frac{2^{\alpha-1}h^{1-\alpha}}{2^{\alpha-1}-1}
   133	  \]
   134	  for $\alpha > 1$. Since $h^{1-\alpha} \le 1$ in the first case, we obtain
   135	  $S(h) \le K_{\alpha,a}B_\alpha(h)$. Combining the near and far bounds, and
   136	  using $B_\alpha(h) \ge 1$, proves the assertion and finiteness of the original
   137	  integral. All constants arose from numerical shell estimates and are
   138	  independent of $d$. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:frequency-row}.
   139	\end{proof}

   141	\begin{corollary}[A time exponent above one half]\label{C:frequency-time}
   142	  For every
   143	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variance-beta-range}
   144	    \frac12 < \beta < \min\left(1-\frac a2,
   145	    \frac{3-a-\alpha}{2}\right),
   146	  \end{equation}
   147	  there is a finite $K_\beta = K_\beta(\alpha,a,\gamma,\beta)$ such that
   148	  \begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-time-bound}
   149	    h^{2-a}\sup_\xi J_h(\xi) \le K_\beta C h^{2\beta},
   150	    \qquad 0 < h \le 1.
   151	  \end{equation}
   152	\end{corollary}
   153	
   154	\begin{proof}
   155	  Both upper endpoints in~\eqref{E:variance-beta-range} exceed one half, by $a <
   156	  1$ and $\alpha+a < 2$. If $\alpha < 1$, use $2-a > 2\beta$ in
   157	  Proposition~\ref{P:frequency-row}. If $\alpha > 1$, use $3-a-\alpha > 2\beta$.
   158	  For $\alpha = 1$, set $\delta = 2-a-2\beta > 0$ and $u = \log(1/h)$. Then
   159	  \[
   160	    h^\delta(1+\log(1/h))
   161	    = e^{-\delta u}(1+u) \le 1+\frac1{e\delta}.
   162	  \]
   163	  This absorbs the critical logarithm. No endpoint value of $\beta$ is used.
   164	  This proves Corollary~\ref{C:frequency-time}.
   165	\end{proof}

   167	\subsection{Forms on the full phase}

   169	Choose and fix $T > 0$. Set $\Lambda = (1-\Delta)^{1/2}$, $s = 1/2$ and $E_r =

   212	\begin{proposition}[Form and phase kernel]\label{P:actual-wave-form}

   264

   266	  Schwartz-valued function on $I$ by time partitions with frozen spatial values,

   277	  convergence in their spectral $H_a$ norms. Multiplication by the fixed

   279	  differences converge in the $\mu$ spectral norm too. The preceding
   280	  compact-support estimate also gives convergence in the original completion.

281	  Hence, the auxiliary extension and original-noise limit agree on these
   282	  products. Constants for this admission argument may depend on $R$; they are
   283	  not the uniform variance constants below.
   284	
   285	  For real tensor tests $f,g$, the Hermitian symmetry of their spatial
   286	  transforms gives
   287	  \[
   288	    A(-\xi) = \overline{A(\xi)},\qquad

   295	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variance-complex-noise}

   306	  2^{|r|/2}\langle\xi-\eta\rangle^{|r|}$ and weighted Schwartz decay reduce this

   308	  $E$ on compact time intervals, directly by its weighted Fourier entries. Thus,
   309	  the ordinary first-response integral exists on states. Since $S(-t)(0,f) =

   313	  this adjoint in $G_w$ is the correctly observed form; $D_\chi$ need not be

   315	  positive-width source with the original noise or assert a source limit.

   346	\begin{lemma}[Hilbert-valued finite Bessel inequality]\label{L:phase-bessel}
   347	  Let $H$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, let $\{u_k\}$ be a finite
   348	  orthonormal family in $L^2(\R^d;\mathbb{C}^2)$, and let $g = (g_1,g_2) \in
   349	  L^2(\R^d;H^2)$. Then
   350	  \begin{equation}\label{E:phase-bessel}
   351	    \sum_k\left\|\int\sum_{j=1}^2u_{k,j}(\eta)g_j(\eta)\ud\eta\right\|_H^2
   352	    \le \int\sum_{j=1}^2\|g_j(\eta)\|_H^2\ud\eta.
   353	  \end{equation}
   354	  The same bound holds with $\overline{u_{k,j}}$ in place of $u_{k,j}$.
   355	\end{lemma}
   356	
   357	\begin{proof}
   358	  Expand $g$ in a countable orthonormal basis of $H$. On each scalar coefficient
   359	  apply scalar Bessel to the orthonormal family $\{\overline{u_k}\}$, or to
   360	  $\{u_k\}$ for the conjugated version. Scalar finite Bessel follows by
   361	  subtracting an orthogonal finite projection and expanding its nonnegative
   362	  squared norm. Sum over the $H$ basis and use Parseval and nonnegative Tonelli.
   363	  The Bochner integrals exist by $L^2$ Cauchy--Schwarz. A finite-dimensional $H$
   364	  uses its finite basis, and the zero space is immediate. No independence is
   365	  involved. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:phase-bessel}.
   366	\end{proof}

   465	\begin{proposition}[Column and adjoint-column maps]\label{P:wave-square-columns}

   486	  Fourier coordinates, replace $g(\xi)$ by $(g(\xi)+\overline{g(-\xi)})/2$, and

   488	  and Gram--Schmidt preserves that class. The same density holds in
   489	  $E_{s-\gamma}$.

   347	\begin{lemma}[Correlated trigonometric products]\label{L:masked-trig-products}
   348	  Let $r,\rho \ge 0$. Let $P_r$ be either $\cos(rt)$ or $\sin(rt)$, and let
   349	  $Q_\rho$ be either $\cos(\rho t)$ or $\sin(\rho t)$. With the amplitude and
   350	  constant above,
   351	  \begin{align}
   352	    \|1_IAP_rQ_\rho\|_a^2
   353	    &\le C_0(a)h^{2-a}(M+hD)^2\mathcal{Q}_h(r,\rho),
   354	    \label{E:masked-trig-products}\\
   355	    \mathcal{Q}_h(r,\rho)
   356	    &:= \langle h(r-\rho)\rangle^{a-1}
   357	    +\langle h(r+\rho)\rangle^{a-1}.
   358	    \label{E:masked-frequency-pair}
   359	  \end{align}
   360	\end{lemma}
   361	
   362	\begin{proof}
   363	  Expanding the two trigonometric factors gives four complex exponential modes
   364	  with frequencies $\sigma r+\tau\rho$, $\sigma,\tau \in \{-1,1\}$, and
   365	  coefficients of absolute value $1/4$. In a Hilbert space,
   366	  \[
   367	    \left\|\sum_j c_jv_j\right\|^2
   368	    \le \left(\sum_j|c_j|\right)\sum_j|c_j|\|v_j\|^2.
   369	  \]

   371	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-temporal-modulation} to each mode. Two frequencies have
   372	  absolute value $|r-\rho|$ and two have absolute value $r+\rho$. This gives one
   373	  half of the asserted right side, and hence the bound. Repeated or zero
   374	  frequencies are permitted; no orthogonality or independence of the modes is
   375	  used. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:masked-trig-products}.

   378	\begin{lemma}[Continuous sine factors]\label{L:masked-continuous-wave}
   379	  Define $c_r(t) = \cos(rt)$ and
   380	  \[
   381	    b_r(t) = \langle r\rangle\frac{\sin(rt)}r\quad(r > 0),
   382	    \qquad b_0(t) = t.
   383	  \]
   384	  For $F_r \in \{c_r,b_r\}$ and $G_\rho \in \{c_\rho,b_\rho\}$,
   385	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-continuous-wave}

   387	    \le C_1(a)(1+T)^4h^{2-a}\mathcal{Q}_h(r,\rho),

   394	  \le r \le 1$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives
   395	  \[
   396	    b_r(t) = t\langle r\rangle\int_0^1\cos(vrt)\ud v.
   397	  \]

   399	  absolute value at most two times a normalized integral of

     4	We first state the Gaussian geometry with its exact covariance scale. Let $H$ be
     5	real separable Hilbert, $W$ its given isonormal process, and $X$ a strongly
     6	measurable centered Gaussian variable in a real separable Banach space
     7	$\mathscr{B}$, with $\E\|X\|^2 < \infty$. Assume every continuous linear
     8	coordinate has the form $\ell(X) = W(k_\ell)$, $k_\ell \in H$. Fix $0 < \delta <
     9	1$ and write
    10	\begin{equation}\label{E:tube-covariance-scale}
    11	  Ch=\E[XW(h)]=\sqrt\delta\,\mathcal{M}_\delta h,\qquad
    12	  H_{\rm seen}=\overline{\operatorname{span}\{k_\ell\}},\qquad
    13	  E_0=\overline{C(H)} .
    14	\end{equation}
    15	Assume $\mathcal{M}_\delta:H \to \mathscr{B}$ is compact. All Hilbert balls
    16	below are closed.
    17	
    18	\subsection{The Wiener-space realization}
    19	
    20	\begin{proposition}[First Wiener chaos realization on the support]
    21	  \label{P:tube-wiener-realization}
    22	  The variable $X$ lies in $E_0$ almost surely, with a centered Radon Gaussian
    23	  law of full support there. Its Cameron space and norm are
    24	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-cameron-space}
    25	    H_{\rm CM}=C(H_{\rm seen}),\qquad
    26	    \|Ch\|_{\rm CM}=\|P_{\rm seen}h\|_H .
    27	  \end{equation}
    28	  This support triple is an abstract Wiener realization, including the
    29	  measurable-norm condition.
    30	\end{proposition}
    31	
    32	\begin{proof}
    33	  The zero law has $C = 0$ and $E_0 = \{0\}$ and is immediate. A countable
    34	  norming family exists in $\mathscr{B}^*$: choose a dense sequence on the unit
    35	  sphere and apply Hahn--Banach at each point. Approximation gives $\|x\| =
    36	  \sup_j|\ell_j(x)|$. Norms of differences from a countable dense set show that
    37	  these coordinates generate the Borel sets. Consequently, $X$ is measurable in
    38	  the completion of $\sigma(W(H))$. Fix an orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ of $H$ and
    39	  set $\mathcal{G}_j = \sigma(W(e_1),\ldots,W(e_j))$. In finite dimension these
    40	  sums and projections stabilize at the dimension. Bochner conditional
    41	  expectations need no Radon--Nikodym property here: define them first on
    42	  finite-valued simple variables using scalar conditional expectations, then
    43	  extend by the $L^2$ norm contraction. Simple approximation supplies their
    44	  scalar testing identities. Gaussian regression and the countable norming
    45	  family give
    46	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-finite-regression}
    47	    X_j=\E[X\mid\mathcal{G}_j]
    48	    =\sum_{l\le j}W(e_l)Ce_l,\qquad X_j\longrightarrow X
    49	    \quad\hbox{in }L^2(\mathscr{B}).
    50	  \end{equation}
    51	  To justify convergence, finite-coordinate scalar events approximate all events
    52	  in the generated sigma field: the class of events whose indicators are
    53	  approximable in $L^2$ is a monotone class containing the finite-coordinate
    54	  algebra. Approximate a Bochner variable by simple variables and use the
    55	  conditional $L^2$ contraction.
    56	
    57	  Bounded testing gives $\ell(Ch) = \langle k_\ell,h\rangle$. Thus, $\ker C =
    58	  H_{\rm seen}^\perp$, and $C$ is injective on $H_{\rm seen}$. The closed first
    59	  Wiener chaos generated by $X$ is exactly $W(H_{\rm seen})$. Its covariance
    60	  image therefore has the first Wiener chaos norm
    61	  in~\eqref{E:tube-cameron-space}; unused directions are removed by the
    62	  orthogonal projection, without an inverse covariance. This is the Cameron
    63	  image under the first Wiener chaos definition. The finite sums
    64	  in~\eqref{E:tube-finite-regression} lie in $E_0$, so $L^2$ convergence and an
    65	  almost-sure subsequence put $X$ in that closed space almost surely.
    66	  Functionals on $E_0$ extend to $\mathscr{B}$ by Hahn--Banach, so restriction
    67	  preserves the scalar laws and first chaos.
    68	
    69	  Its law is tight. For each radius $2^{-j}$ choose a finite union of balls of
    70	  mass greater than $1-\varepsilon2^{-j-1}$, using a countable cover of the
    71	  separable space. The intersection of the corresponding finite closed unions is
    72	  closed and totally bounded and has mass at least $1-\varepsilon$. Completeness
    73	  makes it compact. Metric Borel regularity on these compact sets, followed by
    74	  tightness, gives a Radon law. To prove full support, the tail $X-X_j$ is
    75	  independent of the finite Gaussian sum: every tail coordinate has label
    76	  $(I-P_j)k_\ell$, orthogonal to $e_1,\ldots,e_j$. Joint Gaussianity and
    77	  countable Borel coordinates give Banach tail independence. Given $h$ and
    78	  $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $j$ with $\|CP_jh-Ch\| < \varepsilon/3$ and
    79	  $\mathbb{P}(\|X-X_j\| < \varepsilon/3) > 0$. The finite sum has positive
    80	  probability in every ball about $CP_jh$, even if its covariance is singular:
    81	  the preimage under its finite linear map contains an open ball about the
    82	  coefficient vector of $P_jh$. Independence proves positivity of every ball
    83	  about $Ch$. Closure proves that the support is all of $E_0$.
    84	
    85	  We check the measurable norm explicitly. In $H_{\rm seen}$ put $V_j =
    86	  \operatorname{span}\{P_{\rm seen}e_l:l\le j\}$. Any finite orthonormal family
    87	  $(h_k)$ in $V_j^\perp$ is also orthogonal to $e_1,\ldots,e_j$. The same
    88	  regression and Bochner Jensen argument gives
    89	  \[
    90	    \E[X-X_j\mid W(h_k),\hbox{ all }k]
    91	    =\sum_k W(h_k)Ch_k,\qquad
    92	    \E\left\|\sum_kW(h_k)Ch_k\right\|^2
    93	    \le\E\|X-X_j\|^2 .
    94	  \]
    95	  For any $\varepsilon > 0$ choose $j$ so that the right side is less than
    96	  $\varepsilon^3$. Markov bounds the probability that this finite sum has norm
    97	  exceeding $\varepsilon$ by $\varepsilon$, uniformly over every such finite
    98	  orthonormal family. Since $C:H_{\rm seen} \to H_{\rm CM}$ is isometric, the
    99	  excluded finite-dimensional Cameron subspace is $C(V_j)$. This is the
   100	  measurable-norm tail condition for the dense Hilbert image, whose Banach
   101	  completion is $E_0$. The characteristic functional of the law is $\E
   102	  e^{i\ell(X)} = \exp(-\|k_\ell\|_H^2/2)$. These facts give the stated abstract
   103	  Wiener realization. The zero space has the direct zero-law interpretation.
   104	  This proves Proposition~\ref{P:tube-wiener-realization}.
   105	\end{proof}

   107	\subsection{Closed Gaussian enlargements and the quadratic cost}
   108	
   109	We import the set-enlargement
   110	theorem~\cite{friz.hairer:20:course}*{Theorem~11.6, p.~190}, with footnote~3 on
   111	p.~190; p.~191 supplies the following context. For an abstract Wiener space, a
   112	Borel $A$ of positive mass and its Cameron unit ball $\mathcal{K}$, it states
   113	\[
   114	  \mu((A+t\mathcal{K})^c)
   115	  \le\overline{\Phi}_{\rm N}(\widehat{a}+t),\qquad
   116	  \widehat{a}=\Phi_{\rm N}^{-1}(\mu(A)),\quad t\ge0 .
   117	\]
   118	Here $\Phi_{\rm N}$ is the standard normal distribution function; the same page
   119	gives $\overline{\Phi}_{\rm N}(y) \le e^{-y^2/2}$ for $y \ge 0$. This theorem is
   120	imported, not proved here. It concerns Gaussian input sets, not Gaussianity of a
   121	nonlinear wave. We verify Borel measurability of every enlargement we use.
   122	
   123	\begin{lemma}[Compact images and attained tube radii]
   124	  \label{L:tube-closed-geometry}
   125	  Suppose the law of $X$ is nonzero and put
   126	  \[
   127	    b_\delta=2\E\|X\|,\qquad
   128	    A_\delta=\{x\in E_0:\|x\|\le b_\delta\},\qquad
   129	    \mathcal{T}_r=A_\delta+\mathcal{M}_\delta(\overline{B}_H(r)).
   130	  \]
   131	  Every $\mathcal{T}_r$ is closed. The extended distance $d_\delta(x) =
   132	  \inf\{r\ge0:x\in\mathcal{T}_r\}$ satisfies
   133	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-attained-radius}
   134	    \{d_\delta\le r\}=\mathcal{T}_r,\qquad
   135	    \mathbb{P}(d_\delta(X)>r)\le e^{-r^2/(2\delta)},\quad r\ge0 .
   136	  \end{equation}
   137	  In particular, $d_\delta$ is lower semicontinuous and finite almost surely.
   138	\end{lemma}
   139	
   140	\begin{proof}
   141	  A compact map from a separable Hilbert space sends a closed bounded ball to a
   142	  compact set, including closedness of the image. Indeed, diagonal orthonormal
   143	  coordinates and Fatou give a weakly convergent subsequence of any bounded
   144	  sequence, with limit still in the ball. Compactness gives norm-convergent
   145	  image subsequences, and bounded scalar testing identifies every limit with the
   146	  image of that weak limit. This proves sequential compactness. Closed
   147	  $A_\delta$ plus a compact image is closed: along a converging sequence of
   148	  sums, extract the compact component and pass the residual into the closed base
   149	  set.
   150	
   151	  Membership in $\mathcal{T}_r$ implies $d_\delta \le r$. Conversely, if
   152	  $d_\delta(x) \le r$, choose $h_j$ with $\|h_j\| \le r+1/j$ and
   153	  $x-\mathcal{M}_\delta h_j \in A_\delta$. A weak subsequence has limit $h$ of
   154	  norm at most $r$; compactness gives $\mathcal{M}_\delta h_j \to
   155	  \mathcal{M}_\delta h$. Closedness of the residual proves membership in
   156	  $\mathcal{T}_r$. This also covers $r = 0$ and proves least finite-radius
   157	  attainment. Closed sublevels give lower semicontinuity and Borel
   158	  measurability.
   159	
   160	  The nonzero law has $b_\delta > 0$, and Markov gives $\mu(A_\delta) \ge 1/2$.
   161	  Projection onto $H_{\rm seen}$ removes all unused directions in the original
   162	  covariance space, so~\eqref{E:tube-cameron-space} gives the exact set
   163	  identities
   164	  \[
   165	    \mathcal{K}=C(\overline{B}_H(1))
   166	    =\sqrt\delta\,\mathcal{M}_\delta(\overline{B}_H(1)),\qquad
   167	    \mathcal{T}_r=A_\delta+(r/\sqrt\delta)\mathcal{K} .
   168	  \]
   169	  These are Borel enlargements by the preceding closedness. The imported theorem
   170	  applies to the realization in Proposition~\ref{P:tube-wiener-realization}.
   171	  Since $\widehat{a} \ge 0$, it yields~\eqref{E:tube-attained-radius}. The value
   172	  $\widehat{a} = +\infty$ is allowed when $\mu(A_\delta) = 1$. The tail tends to
   173	  zero, proving almost-sure finiteness. The Cameron embedding does not change
   174	  the factor one half in the Gaussian cost. This proves
   175	  Lemma~\ref{L:tube-closed-geometry}.
   176	\end{proof}

   180	\begin{proposition}[Comparison with the Rayleigh integral, including jumps and zero law]
   181	  \label{P:tube-rayleigh-transfer}
   182	  Let $F:E_0 \to \R$ be Borel and let $G:[0,\infty) \to \R$ be Borel and
   183	  nondecreasing. If $F(x) \le G(r)$ for every $x \in \mathcal{T}_r$ and every $r
   184	  \ge 0$, then
   185	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-rayleigh-transfer}
   186	    \E e^{F(X)/\delta}
   187	    \le\int_0^\infty\frac r\delta
   188	    \exp\left(\frac{G(r)-r^2/2}{\delta}\right)\ud r .
   189	  \end{equation}
   190	  For zero law use $E_0 = \{0\}$, $C = \mathcal{M}_\delta = 0$; the same
   191	  conclusion holds when $F(0) \le G(0)$.
   192	\end{proposition}
   193	
   194	\begin{proof}
   195	  The auxiliary Rayleigh variable $\mathcal{R}_\delta$ with density
   196	  $(r/\delta)e^{-r^2/(2\delta)}$, $r > 0$, has mass one and survival function
   197	  $e^{-r^2/(2\delta)}$ by direct integration. It is a scalar stochastic
   198	  dominator, not a norm of a Gaussian variable in the covariance Hilbert space.
   199	  For every level $t \ge 0$, the upper level set of $e^{G(r)/\delta}$ is an
   200	  upper interval, possibly empty or the whole halfline. An open endpoint is
   201	  controlled by~\eqref{E:tube-attained-radius}. At a positive closed endpoint
   202	  $c$, let $s\uparrow c$:
   203	  \[
   204	    \mathbb{P}(d_\delta(X)\ge c)
   205	    =\lim_{s\uparrow c}\mathbb{P}(d_\delta(X)>s)
   206	    \le e^{-c^2/(2\delta)}
   207	    =\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{R}_\delta\ge c).
   208	  \]
   209	  Rayleigh has no atoms, and at the closed endpoint zero both probability bounds
   210	  are one. On the null event $\{d_\delta(X)=\infty\}$ define
   211	  $e^{G(d_\delta(X))/\delta}$ to be one. No value of $G$ at infinity is needed
   212	  and no expectation changes. Layer cake and Tonelli therefore order the
   213	  expectations of $e^{G(d_\delta(X))/\delta}$ and
   214	  $e^{G(\mathcal{R}_\delta)/\delta}$, even when $G$ jumps or expectations are
   215	  infinite. Least-radius attainment gives $F(X) \le G(d_\delta(X))$ almost
   216	  surely. No measurable selection of a control or residual is needed. This
   217	  proves~\eqref{E:tube-rayleigh-transfer}. For zero law, $X = 0$ and $F(0) \le
   218	  G(0) \le G(r)$; normalization of the Rayleigh density proves the claim
   219	  directly. In particular, $F(0)$ need not be zero. This proves
   220	  Proposition~\ref{P:tube-rayleigh-transfer}.
   221	\end{proof}

   248	\begin{proposition}[Eligibility of the E law]\label{P:tube-actual-law}
   249	  The tuple $X_\delta = (X_m)$ satisfies the preceding Gaussian hypotheses with
   250	  $H = H_I$ and
   251	  \begin{align}
   252	    (\mathcal{M}_\delta\Phi)_m(u)
   253	    &=\int_0^{\min(u,\ell_m)}
   254	    S_E(-v)\mathcal{T}_R\Phi(s_m+\delta v)S_E(v)\ud v,
   255	    \label{E:tube-actual-mean}\\

256	    \E[X_\delta W(\Phi)]&=\sqrt\delta\,\mathcal{M}_\delta\Phi .
   257	    \label{E:tube-actual-covariance}

   260	  \mathscr{B}_\delta$, where $C_\delta\Phi = \E[X_\delta W(\Phi)] =
   261	  \sqrt\delta\,\mathcal{M}_\delta\Phi$. The map $\mathcal{M}_\delta$ is compact
   262	  at each fixed radius and parameters. At $R = R_\delta$,
   263	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-typical-radius}
   264	    b_\delta=2\E\|X_\delta\|_{\delta,p}
   265	    \le C_{Q,B,p}\delta^{(1-a)/2-d/Q}\longrightarrow0 .

   270	  Compact operators on separable Hilbert $E$ form a separable operator-norm
   271	  space: finite-rank rational matrices in an orthonormal basis are dense.
   272	  Polygonal paths give separability of the little H\"older closure. The
   273	  construction is a $C^\theta$ limit of Lipschitz finite coefficient paths
   274	  starting at zero; stopping at $\ell_m$ and extending constantly preserves this
   275	  space and gives zero for an empty final interval. Gaussian transfer retains
   276	  the given $W$ for all finitely many blocks. Every finite collection of linear
   277	  statistics is an $L^2$ limit of joint first Wiener chaos Gaussians, hence
   278	  jointly centered Gaussian. The finite tuple has finite $L^2$ norm by the
   279	  fixed-parameter path moments in Corollary~\ref{C:radius-covariance-residuals}.
   280	  The original Hilbert space $H_I$ is separable by
   281	  Lemma~\ref{L:cameron-supported-tensor}. No separability of all
   282	  $\mathcal{L}(E)$ or full $C^\theta$ is claimed.
   283	
   284	  The $E$ mean field $\mathcal{T}_R$ is the compression of
   285	  Proposition~\ref{P:cameron-full-mean}; it is compact into
   286	  $L^{r_t}(I;\mathcal{K}(E))$ at fixed $R$.
   287	  Proposition~\ref{P:uniform-mean-regulator} gives $\|\mathcal{T}_R\| \le C_{\rm
   288	  mean} = M_0\|C_t\|$ independently of $R \ge 1$. Compact conjugation, affine
   289	  time pullback and $1-1/r_t > \theta$ make the primitive
   290	  in~\eqref{E:tube-actual-mean} bounded from that field space to
   291	  $\mathscr{B}_\delta$, with constant stopping. Composition proves compactness
   292	  of $\mathcal{M}_\delta$. There is no uniform-radius compactness assertion.
   293	
   294	  The rank-zero identity~\eqref{E:cameron-actual-covariance}, compressed to $E$
   295	  as in Proposition~\ref{P:symplectic-block-mean},
   296	  gives~\eqref{E:tube-actual-covariance}. Its scale is exactly
   297	  $g_\delta\delta^{a/2} = \sqrt\delta$. Every stopped row's slow pullback lies
   298	  in $H_I$ by the inside-$I$ endpoint approximation of
   299	  Lemma~\ref{L:cameron-actual-residual}. Countable matrix coordinates and
   300	  rational times identify the tuple in the closed first Wiener chaos $W(H_I)$,

   302	  at $J = 0$ on $F$ and compose any $E$-tuple statistic with the bounded
   303	  $E$-compression. This is same-$W$ covariance, without a block-independence
   304	  assumption or a time-indicator multiplier on the covariance space.
   305	  Proposition~\ref{P:tube-wiener-realization} therefore applies to this exact
   306	  law on its support. Finally, Proposition~\ref{P:radius-mean-anchor}, with zero

   310	  baseline do not replace this global $H_I$ action or get summed as separate
   311	  costs. Zero covariance gives zero operator paths and means directly. This
   312	  proves Proposition~\ref{P:tube-actual-law}.

   315	\begin{lemma}[The endpoint functional]\label{L:tube-actual-endpoint}
   316	  For every $x \in \mathscr{B}_\delta$ define
   317	  \[
   318	    \begin{aligned}
   319	      P_m(x_m)&=S_E(\ell_m)U_{x_m}(\ell_m,0),\qquad
   320	      \mathcal{P}_\delta(x)=P_N(x_N)\cdots P_0(x_0),\\
   321	      F_\delta(x)&=2\delta\log\max(1,\|\mathcal{P}_\delta(x)\|).

   325	  satisfies
   326	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-global-endpoint}
   327	    \mathcal{P}_\delta(X_\delta)
   328	    =P_{\delta,E}^R(L_\delta,0),\qquad
   329	    e^{F_\delta(X_\delta)/\delta}
   330	    =\|P_{\delta,E}^R(L_\delta,0)\|^2 .
   331	  \end{equation}

   333	  without a simultaneous event over all parameter choices.

   338	  $C^\theta$ operator path. Finite products, fixed-time free factors, norm and
   339	  $\log\max(1,\cdot)$ preserve continuity. Thus, $F_\delta$ is defined even off
   340	  every Gaussian full-measure set. Every $x_m$ in this ambient space is a
   341	  compact-valued $C^\theta$ path starting at zero. The finite-product assertion
   342	  of Lemma~\ref{L:symplectic-free} gives, for every such tuple,
   343	  \[
   344	    \|\mathcal{P}_\delta(x)\|
   345	    \ge\left\|S_E\Big(\sum_{m=0}^N\ell_m\Big)\right\|\ge1 .
   346	  \]

   350	  the exact objects, use its single regularized slow noise preserving the given
   351	  noise and pull it back by $T_{\delta,0}$ and $T_{\delta,m}$. At fixed $\delta$

   375	\begin{proposition}[Coarse tube envelope and operator moment]
   376	  \label{P:tube-coarse-envelope}
   377	  On the support $E_{0,\delta}$ let $A_\delta$ be its closed ball of radius
   378	  $b_\delta$ and put
   379	  \[
   380	    G_\delta(r)=
   381	    \sup_{\substack{a\in A_\delta\\\|\Phi\|_{H_I}\le r}}
   382	    F_\delta(a+\mathcal{M}_\delta\Phi).
   383	  \]
   384	  This is finite, nondecreasing and Borel. There is $C_{\rm env} < \infty$,
   385	  independent of $\delta$ and $R \ge 1$, such that
   386	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-coarse-envelope}
   387	    G_\delta(r)\le C_{\rm env}(1+b_\delta^\nu+r^\nu),\qquad
   388	    \E\|P_{\delta,E}^R(L_\delta,0)\|^2
   389	    \le\int_0^\infty\frac r\delta
   390	    e^{(G_\delta(r)-r^2/2)/\delta}\ud r .
   391	  \end{equation}
   392	\end{proposition}
   393	
   394	\begin{proof}
   395	  Put $G_B = \sup_{|v|\le B}\|S_E(v)\|$ and $C_{\rm pr} =
   396	  G_B^2[B^{1-1/r_t}+B^{1-1/r_t-\theta}]$. The lower bound $G_B \ge 1$ follows
   397	  directly from $S_E(0) = I$. Proposition~\ref{P:uniform-actual-cameron} gives
   398	  $1 \le G_B \le 3B$, $C_{\rm pr} \le 18B^{3-1/r_t}$. Its primitive estimate,
   399	  now without the covariance factor $\sqrt\delta$, gives
   400	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-primitive-sum}
   401	    \delta\sum_m h_m^{r_t}
   402	    \le(C_{\rm pr}C_{\rm mean})^{r_t}\|\Phi\|_{H_I}^{r_t},
   403	    \qquad h_m=\|(\mathcal{M}_\delta\Phi)_m\|_{C^\theta}.
   404	  \end{equation}
   405	  Indeed, each primitive norm is at most $C_{\rm pr}\delta^{-1/r_t}
   406	  \|\mathcal{T}_R\Phi\|_{L^{r_t}(I_m)}$. Raising to $r_t$ cancels the $\delta$
   407	  weight, and the true partition sums to the full field norm, including an empty
   408	  cell.
   409	
   410	  The generic Banach Young bound supplies $c_Y = c_Y(B,\theta) > 0$ with
   411	  $\log\|U_d(u,0)\| \le c_Y(1+\|d\|_{C^\theta}^{\nu})$ for $u \le B$. This
   412	  follows from~\eqref{E:young-upper-refined-growth}
   413	  and~\eqref{E:constant-young-growth} by $d \le 1+d^\nu$ and $(1+d)^\nu \le
   414	  2^{\nu-1}(1+d^\nu)$. It applies on $\mathcal{L}(E)$ with multiplication norm
   415	  one, without Gaussian, positivity or Hamiltonian assumptions on $d$. For $a
   416	  \in A_\delta$ put $v_m = \|a_m\|_{C^\theta}$ and $n = N+1$. Convexity and
   417	  submultiplicativity give
   418	  \[
   419	    F_\delta(a+\mathcal{M}_\delta\Phi)
   420	    \le2\delta n(\log G_B+c_Y)
   421	    +2^\nu c_Y\delta\sum_m(v_m^\nu+h_m^\nu).
   422	  \]
   423	  The upper expression is nonnegative, so it also bounds the logarithm with the
   424	  maximum at one. The exact finite weighted power-mean inequalities are
   425	  \begin{align*}
   426	    \delta\sum_m v_m^\nu
   427	    &\le(\delta n)^{1-\nu/p}\|a\|_{\delta,p}^\nu,\\
   428	    \delta\sum_m h_m^\nu
   429	    &\le(\delta n)^{1-\nu/r_t}
   430	    \left(\delta\sum_m h_m^{r_t}\right)^{\nu/r_t}.
   431	  \end{align*}
   432	  They use exponents $p/\nu \ge 1$, $r_t/\nu > 1$ and nonnegative inputs
   433	  $v_m^\nu,h_m^\nu$, followed by positive powers. Zero norms and empty cells
   434	  cause no negative powers; $\delta > 0$ and $n \ge 2$, including the case $p =
   435	  \nu$. Since $\delta n \le 2/B$, these bounds and~\eqref{E:tube-primitive-sum}
   436	  give $F_\delta(a+\mathcal{M}_\delta\Phi) \le D_0+D_1b_\delta^\nu+D_2r^\nu$,
   437	  where
   438	  \begin{align*}
   439	    D_0&=2(2/B)(\log G_B+c_Y),\\
   440	    D_1&=2^\nu c_Y(2/B)^{1-\nu/p},\\
   441	    D_2&=2^\nu c_Y(2/B)^{1-\nu/r_t}
   442	    (C_{\rm pr}C_{\rm mean})^\nu .
   443	  \end{align*}
   444	  Hence, $C_{\rm env} = 1+D_0+D_1+D_2$ is independent of $\delta,R$ and proves
   445	  the coarse bound for every admissible $\delta$, not just when $b_\delta$ is
   446	  small. The supremum sets are nonempty and this bound makes their suprema
   447	  finite. Monotonicity gives Borel measurability without asserting attainment of
   448	  these suprema. The definition bounds $F_\delta$ on every closed tube. Apply
   449	  Proposition~\ref{P:tube-rayleigh-transfer} and~\eqref{E:tube-global-endpoint}
   450	  to obtain the operator-moment bound. For zero law its direct case applies,
   451	  with no assumption that the free endpoint norm is one. This proves
   452	  Proposition~\ref{P:tube-coarse-envelope}.
   453	\end{proof}
   454	
   455	\begin{lemma}[Exact Rayleigh tail bound]\label{L:tube-rayleigh-tail}
   456	  Suppose $G$ is Borel and $G(r) \le A_0+Cr^\nu$, $C \ge 0$, $1 < \nu < 2$. If
   457	  $M > 0$ and $4C \le M^{2-\nu}$, then
   458	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-rayleigh-tail}
   459	    \int_M^\infty\frac r\delta
   460	    e^{(G(r)-r^2/2)/\delta}\ud r
   461	    \le4e^{(A_0-M^2/4)/\delta}.
   462	  \end{equation}
   463	  In particular, the operator-moment bound in~\eqref{E:tube-coarse-envelope} is
   464	  finite at fixed parameters.
   465	\end{lemma}
   466	
   467	\begin{proof}

  5256	  Let $g_{ij}$, $1 \le i \le M$, $1 \le j \le m_i$, be independent standard real
  5257	  Gaussian coordinates, grouped by color $i$, and let $\mathscr{X}$ be a complex
  5258	  Hilbert space. On Gaussian polynomials with coefficients in $\mathscr{X}$ set
  5259	  \[
  5260	    J_i=\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}M_{g_{ij}}\otimes K_{ij},
  5261	  \]
  5262	  where each $K_{ij}$ is bounded on $\mathscr{X}$. Let $F_0,\ldots,F_n$ be
  5263	  bounded operators acting only on $\mathscr{X}$. Fix a word $i_1,\ldots,i_n$,
  5264	  and let $r_i$ be the number of its occurrences of color $i$. If $N_i \ge r_i$
  5265	  and $P$ projects each color onto total Hermite degree at most $N_i$, then, for
  5266	  every $v \in \mathscr{X}$,
  5267	  \begin{equation}\label{E:finite-word-cutoff}
  5268	    \begin{split}
  5269	      &(I\otimes F_n)(PJ_{i_n}P)(I\otimes F_{n-1})\cdots
  5270	      (PJ_{i_1}P)(I\otimes F_0)(1\otimes v)\\
  5271	      &\qquad=(I\otimes F_n)J_{i_n}(I\otimes F_{n-1})\cdots
  5272	      J_{i_1}(I\otimes F_0)(1\otimes v).
  5273	    \end{split}
  5274	  \end{equation}

  5276	  whenever the displayed vector integrals exist.
  5277	\end{lemma}

  5281	  $h_{\boldsymbol a}$ to $\sqrt{a_{ij}+1}\,h_{\boldsymbol a+e_{ij}}
  5282	  +\sqrt{a_{ij}}\,h_{\boldsymbol a-e_{ij}}$; the second term is zero if $a_{ij}
  5283	  = 0$. Thus, it changes the total degree of color $i$ by one and leaves all
  5284	  other color degrees unchanged. The operators $I\otimes F_l$ leave every
  5285	  Gaussian degree unchanged. After the first $l$ insertions, the uncompressed
  5286	  word therefore has color-$i$ degree at most $r_i(l) = |\{j\le l:i_j=i\}| \le
  5287	  r_i \le N_i$. This is an induction starting from degree zero in every color.

  5289	  that word. Induction on $l$ now proves \eqref{E:finite-word-cutoff}. The

  5291	  annihilation and all resulting self-contractions. Linearity and equality of
  5292	  the vector integrands prove the last assertion. This is an equality of

  7450	  \(e^{-2\theta t}\), and adding the second cone, gives the displayed identity.

  7460	      \int_0^\infty\lambda^{a-1}

  7469	  \((\theta+\lambda)^2-\theta^2=\lambda(2\theta+\lambda)\). The smoothing
  7470	  passage is justified by monotone convergence in this nonnegative spectral
  7471	  expression and the finite quadratic form in
  7472	  Lemma~\ref{L:damped-homogeneous-norms}. Alternatively, homogeneity directly
  7473	  bounds the density near zero by a constant times \(\lambda^{a-1}\), and at

    13	\begin{lemma}[Scalar power estimates]\label{L:gaussian-scalar-powers}
    14	  For $0 < \theta < 1$ and $u,v \ge 0$,
    15	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-weighted-power}
    16	    u^\theta v^{1-\theta} \le \theta u+(1-\theta)v.
    17	  \end{equation}
    18	  Consequently, if $L > 0$ and $0 \le q \le L$ are integers, then for real
    19	  $x,y$,
    20	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-integer-power}
    21	    |x|^q|y|^{L-q}
    22	    \le \frac qL|x|^L+\frac{L-q}L|y|^L.
    23	  \end{equation}
    24	  For nonnegative finite sequences, the usual H\"older inequality holds with
    25	  exponents $m$ and $m/(m-1)$, $m > 1$. If $Z \ge 0$ has finite expectation $F$
    26	  and $0 < r < 1$, then $\E Z^r \le F^r$.
    27	\end{lemma}
    28	
    29	\begin{proof}
    30	  If $v > 0$, divide~\eqref{E:gaussian-weighted-power} by $v$ and put $t = u/v$.
    31	  The function $\theta t+1-\theta-t^\theta$ decreases to zero at one and then
    32	  increases, by its derivative $\theta(1-t^{\theta-1})$. Continuity covers $t =
    33	  0$; if $v = 0$ the inequality is immediate. For $0 < q < L$, apply this with
    34	  $u = |x|^L$, $v = |y|^L$ and $\theta = q/L$. The endpoint cases $q = 0,L$ are
    35	  identities, with the ordinary integer convention $a^0 = 1$.
    36	
    37	  To prove finite H\"older, divide the two sequences by their respective
    38	  $\ell^m$ and $\ell^{m/(m-1)}$ norms. If either norm vanishes, the result is
    39	  immediate. Apply~\eqref{E:gaussian-weighted-power} with $\theta = 1/m$ to the
    40	  corresponding normalized powers and sum; the sum of products is at most one.
    41	  Undo the normalization. Finally, $F = 0$ gives $Z = 0$ almost surely. If $F >
    42	  0$, apply \eqref{E:gaussian-weighted-power} to $u = Z/F$, $v = 1$ and $\theta
    43	  = r$, and integrate. The right side has expectation one. This proves
    44	  Lemma~\ref{L:gaussian-scalar-powers}.
    45	\end{proof}

    47	\begin{lemma}[Two Hermitian trace bounds]\label{L:gaussian-trace-bounds}
    48	  Let $B,Y$ be finite Hermitian matrices, $m \ge 2$ an integer, and $L = 2m-2$.
    49	  For integers $0 \le q \le L$,
    50	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-trace-word}
    51	    \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(BY^qBY^{L-q})
    52	    \le \operatorname{Tr}(B^2|Y|^L).
    53	  \end{equation}
    54	  If $D \ge 0$ is Hermitian, then
    55	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gaussian-trace-holder}
    56	    \operatorname{Tr}(D|Y|^{2m-2})
    57	    \le (\operatorname{Tr}D^m)^{1/m}
    58	    (\operatorname{Tr}|Y|^{2m})^{(m-1)/m}.
    59	  \end{equation}
    60	\end{lemma}
    61	
    62	\begin{proof}
    63	  Diagonalize $Y$, with real eigenvalues $\lambda_i$, and write $b_{ij}$ for the
    64	  entries of $B$ in that basis. Hermitian symmetry gives $b_{ji} =
    65	  \overline{b_{ij}}$. The trace word is the real sum
    66	  \[
    67	    \sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2\lambda_j^q\lambda_i^{L-q}.
    68	  \]
    69	  Bound each product by its absolute value and use
    70	  \eqref{E:gaussian-integer-power}. After interchanging $i,j$, the two resulting
    71	  sums agree because $|b_{ij}| = |b_{ji}|$. Each equals
    72	  $\sum_{i,j}|b_{ij}|^2|\lambda_i|^L = \operatorname{Tr}(B^2|Y|^L)$. The two
    73	  weights sum to one, proving \eqref{E:gaussian-trace-word}. No commutation of
    74	  $B$ and $Y$ is used.
    75	
    76	  In the same basis put $d_i = D_{ii} \ge 0$. If $\theta_j$ are the nonnegative
    77	  eigenvalues of $D$, a unitary change of basis gives $d_i =
    78	  \sum_j|U_{ij}|^2\theta_j$. Both row and column sums of $|U_{ij}|^2$ equal one.
    79	  Finite convexity therefore yields
    80	  \[
    81	    \sum_i d_i^m \le \sum_{i,j}|U_{ij}|^2\theta_j^m
    82	    = \operatorname{Tr}D^m.
    83	  \]

    86	  inequality with $s$ equal to the weighted mean. Now apply finite H\"older from
    87	  Lemma~\ref{L:gaussian-scalar-powers} to $\sum_i d_i|\lambda_i|^{2m-2}$. Since
    88	  $(2m-2)m/(m-1) = 2m$, the last display proves \eqref{E:gaussian-trace-holder},

   123	  $\operatorname{Tr}Y^{2m} = \sum_k g_k \operatorname{Tr}(B_kY^{2m-1})$ and
   124	  differentiate the $2m-1$ factors in their order. This gives exactly
   125	  \[

   127	    \E\operatorname{Tr}(B_kY^qB_kY^{L-q}).

   130	  differentiated polynomial is real by conjugation and trace cyclicity. No
