   199	\begin{lemma}[Cutoff factorization]\label{L:cutoff-factorization}
   200	  Choose a cube $Q_L = (-L/2,L/2)^d$ containing $\operatorname{supp}\chi$ in its
   201	  interior, and a real $\psi \in C_c^\infty(Q_L)$ equal to one near
   202	  $\operatorname{supp}\chi$. On the auxiliary torus $\mathbb{T}_L$ use Lebesgue
   203	  measure and the orthonormal basis
   204	  \[
   205	    e_k(x)=L^{-d/2}e^{i\kappa_k\cdot x},\qquad
   206	    \kappa_k=2\pi k/L,\qquad k \in \mathbb{Z}^d,
   207	  \]
   208	  with $\|v\|_{H^r(\mathbb{T}_L)}^2 = \sum_k\langle\kappa_k\rangle^{2r}|v_k|^2$.
   209	  Periodization of $\psi u$ and multiplication of a periodic function by $\chi$
   210	  extend to bounded maps
   211	  \begin{equation}\label{E:cutoff-periodic-maps}
   212	    \mathcal{P}_\psi:H^r(\R^d)\to H^r(\mathbb{T}_L),\qquad
   213	    \mathcal{E}_\chi:H^r(\mathbb{T}_L)\to H^r(\R^d)
   214	  \end{equation}
   215	  for every real $r$. If $\mathcal{I}_\gamma$ denotes the identity inclusion
   216	  from $H^{\sigma+\gamma}(\mathbb{T}_L)$ to $H^\sigma(\mathbb{T}_L)$, then
   217	  \begin{equation}\label{E:cutoff-whole-space-recovery}
   218	    \mathcal{E}_\chi\mathcal{I}_\gamma\mathcal{P}_\psi u=\chi u,
   219	    \qquad u \in H^{\sigma+\gamma}(\R^d).
   220	  \end{equation}
   221	\end{lemma}
   222	
   223	\begin{proof}
   224	  For $x,y \in \R^d$ and real $r$, the elementary inequality $\langle x\rangle
   225	  \le \sqrt{2}\langle y\rangle\langle x-y\rangle$ gives
   226	  \begin{equation}\label{E:cutoff-peetre}
   227	    \left(\frac{\langle x\rangle}{\langle y\rangle}\right)^r
   228	    \le 2^{|r|/2}\langle x-y\rangle^{|r|}.
   229	  \end{equation}
   230	  For negative $r$, interchange $x,y$ before raising to $|r|$. Integration by
   231	  parts gives rapid decay of the Fourier transform of every compact smooth
   232	  cutoff. For any lattice spacing $a > 0$ and $N > d$,
   233	  \begin{equation}\label{E:cutoff-lattice-sum}
   234	    \sup_y\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^d}\langle y-ak\rangle^{-N}<\infty.
   235	  \end{equation}
   236	  Indeed, translate $y$ into a centered lattice cell, where $|y| \le a\sqrt
   237	  d/2$. For $|k| \ge \sqrt d$ we have $|y-ak| \ge a|k|/2$. The remaining terms
   238	  are finite; the tail converges by dyadic lattice counting, since there are at
   239	  most $C_d2^{jd}$ lattice points in the $j$th shell in $k$. More precisely, for
   240	  $|k| \ge \sqrt d$, the preceding inequality gives
   241	  \[
   242	    \langle y-ak\rangle^{-N}
   243	    \le \max(1,2/a)^N\langle k\rangle^{-N}.
   244	  \]
   245	  The comparison-series terms are bounded by $2^{-jN}$ on each dyadic $k$-shell.
   246	  Thus, its convergent geometric sum carries constants depending on $a,d,N$, as
   247	  does~\eqref{E:cutoff-lattice-sum}.
   248	
   249	  We use the mixed Schur bound for a kernel whose absolute row and column
   250	  integrals are bounded by $M_1,M_2$. Weighted Cauchy--Schwarz at each output
   251	  point, followed by Tonelli, bounds its squared operator norm by $M_1M_2$. The
   252	  same proof works with counting measure on one side and Lebesgue measure on the
   253	  other, first on dense finite or compact inputs.
   254	
   255	  For Schwartz $u$, the $k$th coefficient of its cutoff periodization is
   256	  \[
   257	    (\mathcal{P}_\psi u)_k
   258	    = L^{-d/2}\int\psi(x)u(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\ud x
   259	    = L^{-d/2}\int\widehat{\psi}(\kappa_k-\xi)\widehat{u}(\xi)\ud\xi.
   260	  \]
   261	  The $c_d$ from Fourier inversion cancels the $c_d^{-1}$ in the ordinary
   262	  Fourier integral of $\psi$. After weighting, its exact kernel is
   263	  \[
   264	    L^{-d/2}\left(\frac{\langle\kappa_k\rangle}{\langle\xi\rangle}\right)^r
   265	    \widehat{\psi}(\kappa_k-\xi).
   266	  \]
   267	  For a finite torus polynomial $v$, the normalized Fourier kernel of
   268	  $\mathcal{E}_\chi v$ is
   269	  \[
   270	    L^{-d/2}\left(\frac{\langle\xi\rangle}{\langle\kappa_k\rangle}\right)^r
   271	    \widehat{\chi}(\xi-\kappa_k).
   272	  \]
   273	  There is no additional $c_d$ in this kernel. By~\eqref{E:cutoff-peetre}, each
   274	  is bounded in absolute value by a rapidly decreasing function of its frequency
   275	  difference, times a fixed constant. One Schur quantity is its $L^1$ integral
   276	  and the other a uniformly translated lattice sum, bounded
   277	  by~\eqref{E:cutoff-lattice-sum}. This proves~\eqref{E:cutoff-periodic-maps},
   278	  including negative $r$.

   280	  Smooth compact approximation in weighted Fourier $L^2$ proves Schwartz density
   281	  on $\R^d$; weighted sequence truncation proves polynomial density on the
   282	  torus. Hence, these maps extend uniquely. Their distributional meanings follow
   283	  by testing against compact smooth functions and density: each periodic
   284	  coefficient pairs the distribution with a compact smooth test. No point
   285	  sampling of a rough Fourier function is used. The same full-Lebesgue Schur
   286	  argument proves smooth compact multiplication bounded on every whole-space
   287	  $H^r$.

   289	  For Schwartz $u$, the periodic Fourier series of $\psi u$ converges smoothly

   294	  multiplication. Density proves \eqref{E:cutoff-whole-space-recovery} on that
   295	  full domain. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:cutoff-factorization}.
   296	\end{proof}

   359	\subsection{Balanced adjoints and localized variance envelopes}
   360	
   361	For $E = H^{1/2}(\R^d)\times H^{-1/2}(\R^d)$ use the physical unitary
   362	coordinates
   363	\[
   364	  J_0(u,v)=(\Lambda^{1/2}u,\Lambda^{-1/2}v),\qquad
   365	  H=L^2(\R^d;\mathbb{C}^2).
   366	\]
   367	The frequency map $J$ in Section~\ref{S:wave-variance} is
   368	$(\mathcal{F}\oplus\mathcal{F})J_0$. Let $D_\chi$ multiply both phase entries
   369	and define
   370	\begin{align}
   371	  P_\chi&=J_0D_\chi J_0^{-1},\qquad
   372	  D_\gamma=\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda^{-\gamma},\Lambda^{-\gamma}),
   373	  \label{E:compact-balanced-cutoff}\\
   374	  K_{\rm out}&=P_\chi D_\gamma,\qquad
   375	  K_{\rm in}=P_\chi^*D_\gamma.
   376	  \label{E:compact-two-factors}
   377	\end{align}
   378	
   379	\begin{proposition}[Both compact envelopes]\label{P:compact-two-envelopes}
   380	  The operator $P_\chi$ is bounded. For the unitary swap $U(v,w) = (w,v)$,
   381	  \[
   382	    P_\chi^*=UP_\chi U,\qquad K_{\rm in}=UK_{\rm out}U.
   383	  \]
   384	  Both factors are compact and have equal $S_p$ norms for $p \ge 1$, $p\gamma >
   385	  d$. For $p \ge 2$, $p\gamma > d$, the positive compact operators
   386	  \[
   387	    B_{\rm out}=P_\chi D_\gamma^2P_\chi^*=K_{\rm out}K_{\rm out}^*,
   388	    \qquad B_{\rm in}=P_\chi^*D_\gamma^2P_\chi=K_{\rm in}K_{\rm in}^*
   389	  \]
   390	  satisfy
   391	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-envelope-traces}
   392	    \operatorname{Tr}B_{\rm out}^{p/2}
   393	    =\operatorname{Tr}B_{\rm in}^{p/2}=\|K_{\rm out}\|_{S_p}^p.
   394	  \end{equation}
   395	\end{proposition}
   396	
   397	\begin{proof}
   398	  Put $A_\sigma = \Lambda^\sigma\chi\Lambda^{-\sigma}$. The full-Lebesgue Schur
   399	  argument in Lemma~\ref{L:cutoff-factorization} shows boundedness for every
   400	  real $\sigma$. On Schwartz functions, self-adjointness of real multiplication
   401	  and of the Bessel powers gives $A_\sigma^* = A_{-\sigma}$. Density and
   402	  boundedness extend this to the Hilbert adjoints. No evenness of $\chi$ is
   403	  needed. Thus,
   404	  \[
   405	    P_\chi=\operatorname{diag}(A_{1/2},A_{-1/2}),\qquad
   406	    P_\chi^*=\operatorname{diag}(A_{-1/2},A_{1/2})=UP_\chi U.
   407	  \]
   408	  The swap commutes with $D_\gamma$, giving the claimed factor identity. The
   409	  blocks of $K_{\rm out}$ are $K_{\chi,1/2,\gamma}$ and $K_{\chi,-1/2,\gamma}$.
   410	  Proposition~\ref{P:cutoff-singular-values} gives compactness and $S_p$
   411	  membership. The singular values of their direct sum form the multiset union,
   412	  so
   413	  \[
   414	    \|K_{\rm out}\|_{S_p}^p
   415	    =\|K_{\chi,1/2,\gamma}\|_{S_p}^p+
   416	    \|K_{\chi,-1/2,\gamma}\|_{S_p}^p.
   417	  \]
   418	  Unitary conjugation preserves them. Finally, the positive eigenvalues of
   419	  $KK^*$ and $K^*K$ agree with multiplicity: on an eigenspace with eigenvalue
   420	  $\lambda > 0$, the maps $K/\sqrt\lambda$ and $K^*/\sqrt\lambda$ are inverse
   421	  isometries. Zero eigenvalues contribute nothing to the trace. Summing these
   422	  scalar powers proves~\eqref{E:compact-envelope-traces}. This proves
   423	  Proposition~\ref{P:compact-two-envelopes}.
   424	\end{proof}
   425	
   426	We use the usual positive square root of a bounded positive operator and the
   427	spectral decomposition of compact positive operators. The needed order argument
   428	is recorded explicitly.
   429	
   430	\begin{lemma}[Compact positive order and trace]\label{L:compact-positive-order}
   431	  If $A,B$ are bounded self-adjoint operators with $0 \le A \le B$ and $B$
   432	  compact positive, then $A$ is compact and its ordered eigenvalues satisfy
   433	  $\lambda_j(A) \le \lambda_j(B)$, including zero padding. Consequently, for $t
   434	  \ge 1$ with finite $\operatorname{Tr}B^t$,
   435	  \begin{equation}\label{E:compact-positive-trace}
   436	    \operatorname{Tr}A^t\le\operatorname{Tr}B^t.
   437	  \end{equation}
   438	\end{lemma}
   439	
   440	\begin{proof}
   441	  Let $Q_n$ be finite spectral projections of $B$ whose tails tend to zero in
   442	  norm. Then
   443	  \[
   444	    \|(1-Q_n)A^{1/2}\|^2
   445	    =\|(1-Q_n)A(1-Q_n)\|
   446	    \le\|(1-Q_n)B(1-Q_n)\|\longrightarrow0.
   447	  \]
   448	  Thus, $A^{1/2}$ is a norm limit of finite-rank operators and is compact, as is
   449	  $A$. For compact positive operators, the max-min formula for $\lambda_j$
   450	  follows in an eigenbasis: the span of the first $j$ eigenvectors gives the
   451	  lower bound for the supremum over $j$-dimensional subspaces of their minimum
   452	  Rayleigh quotient, while every such subspace meets the orthogonal complement
   453	  of the first $j-1$ eigenvectors, giving the upper bound. Compare the Rayleigh
   454	  quotients of $A$ and $B$ to obtain the eigenvalue inequality. Sum the ordered
   455	  scalar powers to prove \eqref{E:compact-positive-trace}. No inequality $A^t
   456	  \le B^t$ is asserted. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:compact-positive-order}.
   457	\end{proof}
   458	
   459	\begin{proposition}[Localized finite variance bounds]\label{P:localized-finite-variance}
   460	  Suppose finitely many bounded operators $Z_\ell$ on $H$ satisfy
   461	  \begin{equation}\label{E:localized-finite-hypotheses}
   462	    P_\chi Z_\ell=Z_\ell=Z_\ell P_\chi,\qquad
   463	    V_{\rm out}:=\sum_\ell Z_\ell Z_\ell^*\le CD_\gamma^2,\qquad
   464	    V_{\rm in}:=\sum_\ell Z_\ell^*Z_\ell\le CD_\gamma^2,
   465	  \end{equation}
   466	  with $C \ge 0$. If $p \ge 2$ and $p\gamma > d$, every $Z_\ell$ is compact in
   467	  $S_p$, the two variances are compact in $S_{p/2}$, and
   468	  \begin{align}
   469	    V_{\rm out}&\le CB_{\rm out},\qquad V_{\rm in}\le CB_{\rm in},
   470	    \label{E:localized-two-envelopes}\\
   471	    \operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm out}^{p/2},\quad
   472	    \operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm in}^{p/2}
   473	    &\le C^{p/2}\|K_{\rm out}\|_{S_p}^p.
   474	    \label{E:localized-trace-bounds}
   475	  \end{align}
   476	\end{proposition}
   477	
   478	\begin{proof}
   479	  Left localization gives $V_{\rm out} = P_\chi V_{\rm out}P_\chi^*$. Apply
   480	  positive congruence to the output bound
   481	  in~\eqref{E:localized-finite-hypotheses} to get $V_{\rm out} \le CP_\chi
   482	  D_\gamma^2P_\chi^* = CB_{\rm out}$. Right localization similarly gives $V_{\rm
   483	  in} = P_\chi^*V_{\rm in}P_\chi \le CB_{\rm in}$.
   484	  Proposition~\ref{P:compact-two-envelopes} and
   485	  Lemma~\ref{L:compact-positive-order} prove compactness and the two trace
   486	  bounds with $t = p/2$. If $C = 0$, both variances and every $Z_\ell$ vanish,
   487	  so all assertions are immediate.
   488	
   489	  For each $\ell$, $Z_\ell Z_\ell^* \le V_{\rm out}$ is compact by the same
   490	  lemma. Its finite spectral projections $Q_n$ give $\|(1-Q_n)Z_\ell\|^2 =
   491	  \|(1-Q_n)Z_\ell Z_\ell^*(1-Q_n)\| \to 0$. Hence, $Z_\ell$ is compact. Its
   492	  singular values squared are the nonzero eigenvalues of $Z_\ell Z_\ell^*$.
   493	  Comparing with $V_{\rm out}$ and summing proves $Z_\ell \in S_p$ with
   494	  $\|Z_\ell\|_{S_p}^p \le \operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm out}^{p/2}$. This proves
   495	  Proposition~\ref{P:localized-finite-variance}.
   496	\end{proof}
   497	
   498	The two localization identities are hypotheses here; a noise coefficient family
   499	has not yet been shown to satisfy them. In particular, $P_\chi$ is not assumed
   500	self-adjoint or a projection.
   501	
   502	\begin{corollary}[Finite Gaussian operators]\label{C:finite-gaussian-operators}
   503	  Under~\eqref{E:localized-finite-hypotheses}, let $g_\ell$ be independent real
   504	  standard Gaussians. For even $p \ge 2$ with $p\gamma > d$, the finite sum $X =
   505	  \sum_\ell g_\ell Z_\ell$ satisfies
   506	  \begin{equation}\label{E:finite-gaussian-operator-bound}
   507	    (\E\|X\|_{S_p}^p)^{1/p}
   508	    \le\sqrt{p-1}\sqrt C\|K_{\rm out}\|_{S_p}.
   509	  \end{equation}
   510	  Its extended norm is measurable, with finite expectation as displayed.
   511	\end{corollary}
   512	
   513	\begin{proof}
   514	  Choose finite-rank orthogonal projections $\Pi_n$ from a countable orthonormal
   515	  basis of $H$, with $\Pi_n \to I$ strongly. Put $Z_{\ell,n} = \Pi_nZ_\ell\Pi_n$
   516	  and $X_n = \sum_\ell g_\ell Z_{\ell,n}$, viewed as matrices on
   517	  $\operatorname{ran}\Pi_n$. Their output variance satisfies
   518	  \[
   519	    \sum_\ell\Pi_nZ_\ell\Pi_nZ_\ell^*\Pi_n
   520	    \le\Pi_nV_{\rm out}\Pi_n,
   521	  \]
   522	  since the difference is $\sum_\ell\Pi_nZ_\ell(1-\Pi_n)Z_\ell^*\Pi_n \ge 0$.
   523	  The input inequality is identical with adjoints interchanged. Compact max-min
   524	  also gives $\lambda_j(\Pi_nV\Pi_n) \le \lambda_j(V)$ for positive compact $V$,
   525	  since Rayleigh subspaces inside $\operatorname{ran}\Pi_n$ form a subset of all
   526	  subspaces. Thus, both variance trace powers of these matrices are bounded by
   527	  $C^{p/2}\|K_{\rm out}\|_{S_p}^p$.
   528	
   529	  Proposition~\ref{P:finite-gaussian-matrix} applies to these finite complex
   530	  matrices, the same real independent Gaussians and the even $p$. Taking the
   531	  average of the two already bounded trace powers gives
   532	  \begin{equation}\label{E:finite-gaussian-compression-bound}
   533	    \E\|X_n\|_{S_p}^p
   534	    \le(p-1)^{p/2}C^{p/2}\|K_{\rm out}\|_{S_p}^p.
   535	  \end{equation}
   536	  No factor two is added by this average.
   537	
   538	  For each Gaussian coordinate vector, $X$ is a finite sum of compact operators.
   539	  Strong convergence of $\Pi_n$ implies $\Pi_nX\Pi_n \to X$ in operator norm:
   540	  approximate $X$ by a finite-rank $F$, use uniform strong convergence on the
   541	  finite-dimensional ranges of $F$ and $F^*$, and control the remainder using
   542	  $\|\Pi_n\| \le 1$. Singular values are norm-Lipschitz. Indeed, their formula
   543	  \[
   544	    s_j(A)=\inf_{\dim L<j}
   545	    \sup_{v\in L^\perp,\ \|v\|=1}\|Av\|
   546	  \]
   547	  follows from compact singular vectors and gives $s_j(A) \le s_j(B)+\|A-B\|$,
   548	  and the reverse bound by interchanging $A,B$. Hence, $s_j(X_n) \to s_j(X)$ for
   549	  each $j$. Fatou for the nonnegative singular-value sum gives $\|X\|_{S_p}^p
   550	  \le \liminf_n\|X_n\|_{S_p}^p$, allowing extended infinity. These variables are
   551	  measurable: the finite Gaussian coordinate map into operators is
   552	  norm-continuous, each singular value is continuous, and the norm power is
   553	  their nonnegative measurable sum. Fatou in probability
   554	  and~\eqref{E:finite-gaussian-compression-bound} prove the bound and
   555	  almost-sure finiteness. No $S_p$-Bochner convergence is assumed. This proves
   556	  Corollary~\ref{C:finite-gaussian-operators}.
   557	\end{proof}
   558	
   559	\subsection{A nonzero witness and the need for a compact cutoff}
   560	
   561	\begin{proposition}[Whole-space cutoff tests]\label{P:cutoff-boundary-tests}
   562	  If $\chi$ equals one on a nonempty open set, there is a nonzero rank-one
   563	  operator satisfying~\eqref{E:localized-finite-hypotheses} with a finite common
   564	  $C$. On the other hand, $\Lambda^{-\gamma}$ on $L^2(\R^d)$ is not compact for
   565	  any $\gamma > 0$.
   566	\end{proposition}
   567	
   568	\begin{proof}
   569	  Choose nonzero real $v,f \in C_c^\infty$ supported inside the plateau, and put
   570	  $\widetilde{v} = (\Lambda^{1/2}v,0)$ and $\widetilde{w} =
   571	  (\Lambda^{-1/2}f,0)$. Both are Schwartz. The block formulas give
   572	  $P_\chi\widetilde{v} = \widetilde{v}$ and $P_\chi^*\widetilde{w} =
   573	  \widetilde{w}$. Therefore, $Zx = \langle x,\widetilde{w}\rangle\widetilde{v}$
   574	  satisfies $P_\chi Z = Z = ZP_\chi$. Its two variances are
   575	  $\|\widetilde{w}\|^2\widetilde{v}\otimes\widetilde{v}^*$ and
   576	  $\|\widetilde{v}\|^2\widetilde{w}\otimes\widetilde{w}^*$. For any Schwartz $a$
   577	  and any $x \in H$,
   578	  \[
   579	    |\langle x,a\rangle|
   580	    =|\langle D_\gamma x,D_\gamma^{-1}a\rangle|
   581	    \le\|D_\gamma x\|\|D_\gamma^{-1}a\|.
   582	  \]
   583	  The inverse multiplier is applied only to Schwartz $a$, so it belongs to $H$.
   584	  Apply the inequality with $a = \widetilde{v},\widetilde{w}$ to obtain the two
   585	  variance bounds with
   586	  \[
   587	    C=\max\left(
   588	    \|\widetilde{w}\|^2\|D_\gamma^{-1}\widetilde{v}\|^2,
   589	    \|\widetilde{v}\|^2\|D_\gamma^{-1}\widetilde{w}\|^2\right)<\infty.
   590	  \]
   591	  This witness uses a plateau; no nonzero family is inferred for every compact
   592	  cutoff or identified with a source family.
   593	
   594	  For noncompactness, take $f$ with nonzero Gaussian Fourier transform. Then $g
   595	  = \Lambda^{-\gamma}f$ is a nonzero Schwartz function. The images of translates
   596	  of $f$ are the same translates of $g$. With $T_hg(x) = g(x-h)$, Plancherel
   597	  gives
   598	  \[
   599	    \langle T_hg,g\rangle
   600	    =\int e^{-i\xi\cdot h}|\widehat{g}(\xi)|^2\ud\xi
   601	    =c_d^{-1}\widehat{|\widehat{g}|^2}(h).
   602	  \]
   603	  This tends to zero because $|\widehat{g}|^2$ is Schwartz. Choose a large
   604	  spacing so that any two distinct translates in the resulting sequence have
   605	  image distance at least $\|g\|$. The input norms are identical, but the images
   606	  have no Cauchy subsequence. This disproves compactness. This proves
   607	  Proposition~\ref{P:cutoff-boundary-tests}.
   608	\end{proof}
   609	
   610	Thus, the choice $\chi = 1$ cannot be substituted into the compact-cutoff
   611	argument. No necessity at the Schatten endpoint $p\gamma = d$ is asserted. The
   612	results concern finite matrices and conditional finite operator sums.
   613	Coefficient localization, compact variance tails, an infinite Gaussian series
   614	and time regularity are proved in Section~\ref{S:actual-operator-driver}; source
   615	and Young identification are proved in
   616	Sections~\ref{S:source-driver-convergence}--\ref{S:constant-phase-young}. They
   617	are not consequences of the finite comparison alone.

   231	  levels are controlled by unit partitions. The deterministic dyadic chaining
   232	  argument in Lemma~\ref{L:driver-holder-limit} therefore bounds the
   233	  $L^qC^{\eta_t}$ norms by $C_{Q,B}\sqrt q\,R^{d/Q}$. Each finite path is
   234	  continuous and starts at zero, as required there. The fixed-horizon embedding
   235	  $C^{\eta_t}\hookrightarrow C^\theta$ gives the same estimate in $C^\theta$.
   236	
   237	  For each fixed $R$, Lemma~\ref{L:driver-holder-limit} identifies $M_R(W)$ as
   238	  the all-finite-moment $C^\theta$ limit of these very $M_N$. Pass the uniform
   239	  finite-$N$ estimate to this limit. Uniform convergence in $R$ is unnecessary:
   240	  the limiting bound has its explicit radius dependence at every $R$. For
   241	  arbitrary $v \ge 1$, choose an even $q \ge \max(v,Q)$ with $q \le v+Q+2 \le
   242	  (Q+3)v$. Lyapunov's inequality gives~\eqref{E:radius-actual-path-moments},
   243	  absorbing $\sqrt{Q+3}$ into the fixed constant. This proves
   244	  Proposition~\ref{P:radius-actual-moments}.
   245	\end{proof}

   247	\begin{corollary}[Deterministic covariance residuals]
   248	  \label{C:radius-covariance-residuals}
   249	  Let $Y$ be a centered Gaussian linear noise on the coupled space, with
   250	  $\operatorname{Var}Y(f) \le C\|f\|_{H_W}^2$, $C \ge 0$. Its transferred
   251	  operator path satisfies
   252	  \[
   253	    \|M_R(Y)\|_{L^v(C^\theta)}
   254	    \le\sqrt C\,C_{Q,B}\sqrt v\,R^{d/Q}.
   255	  \]

   257	  for any deterministic orthogonal projection $\Pi$ on the slow $H_W$. Its rank
   258	  may be infinite and it may depend on $\delta,R$.

   261	\begin{proof}
   262	  Proposition~\ref{P:source-gaussian-transfer} is a linear Gaussian covariance
   263	  contraction theorem for this same physical mask and these same deterministic
   264	  coefficient maps. It bounds the path norm by $\sqrt C$ times the reference
   265	  isonormal operator-path norm. The reference has the canonical operator-path
   266	  law used in Proposition~\ref{P:radius-actual-moments}; the $Y$ is not replaced
   267	  in this comparison. The zero case gives zero directly. This proves the first
   268	  assertion. For the second, the original isometry \eqref{E:raw-block-pullback},

   270	  $\operatorname{Var}Y_m(f) \le \|f\|_{H_W}^2$, where the right side is the
   271	  original norm in fast coordinates. The joint residuals retain the given slow
   272	  $W$ and may be correlated. They need not lie in the span of an individual fast
   273	  noise, which is not a hypothesis of Gaussian transfer. No random
   274	  noise-dependent projection is used. This proves
   275	  Corollary~\ref{C:radius-covariance-residuals}.

   278	\subsection{The growing-radius expected-norm anchor}
   279	
   280	\begin{proposition}[Averaged block mean tends to zero]
   281	  \label{P:radius-mean-anchor}
   282	  Fix integer $B \ge 1$ and use the true block partition $B,\delta,N,\ell_m$ of
   283	  Section~\ref{S:actual-cameron-mean}, with $0 < \delta < \min(1,1/B)$ and $N =
   284	  \lfloor1/(\delta B)\rfloor$. For $Y_m$ as in
   285	  Corollary~\ref{C:radius-covariance-residuals}, put
   286	  \[
   287	    X_m(u)=g_\delta M_R(Y_m)(\min(u,\ell_m)),\qquad
   288	    Z_\delta=\left(\delta\sum_{m=0}^N
   289	    \|X_m\|_{C^\theta}^p\right)^{1/p},\qquad
   290	    g_\delta=\delta^{(1-a)/2},
   291	  \]
   292	  for any fixed $p \ge 1$. Then
   293	  \begin{equation}\label{E:radius-mean-anchor}
   294	    \E Z_\delta\le(2/B)^{1/p}C_{Q,B}\sqrt p\,
   295	    g_\delta R^{d/Q}.
   296	  \end{equation}
   297	  In particular, for $R_\delta = \delta^{-1}+2$,
   298	  \begin{equation}\label{E:radius-mean-anchor-decay}
   299	    2\E Z_\delta
   300	    \le2(2/B)^{1/p}C_{Q,B}\sqrt p\,3^{d/Q}
   301	    \delta^{e_{\rm anchor}}\longrightarrow0,\qquad
   302	    e_{\rm anchor}=\frac{1-a}{2}-\frac dQ>0 .
   303	  \end{equation}
   304	  Both bounds are uniform in the deterministic orthogonal projection.
   305	\end{proposition}
   306	
   307	\begin{proof}
   308	  Stopping an interaction primitive starting at zero and extending it constantly
   309	  to $B$ does not increase its supremum or H\"older seminorm. An empty last
   310	  interval gives the zero path. Probability normalization and Lyapunov give
   311	  \begin{align*}
   312	    \E Z_\delta
   313	    &\le(\E Z_\delta^p)^{1/p}
   314	    =\left(\delta\sum_{m=0}^N
   315	    \E\|X_m\|_{C^\theta}^p\right)^{1/p}\\
   316	    &\le[\delta(N+1)]^{1/p}g_\delta
   317	    C_{Q,B}\sqrt p\,R^{d/Q}.
   318	  \end{align*}
   319	  This is linearity for a finite sum; no time-block independence or maximum over
   320	  blocks is used. Since $\delta B < 1$, we have $N \ge 1$ and $N+1 \le 2/(\delta
   321	  B)$, proving~\eqref{E:radius-mean-anchor}.
   322	
   323	  Now $R_\delta \le 3/\delta$ because $\delta < 1$. The last condition
   324	  in~\eqref{E:radius-anchor-Q} is equivalent to $Q(1-a) > 2d$. Dividing by $2Q >
   325	  0$ gives $e_{\rm anchor} > 0$. Substitute this radius
   326	  into~\eqref{E:radius-mean-anchor} to
   327	  obtain~\eqref{E:radius-mean-anchor-decay}. The estimate holds at each fixed
   328	  $B,p,Q$ and model, uniformly in every deterministic residual projection. This
   329	  proves Proposition~\ref{P:radius-mean-anchor}.
   330	\end{proof}
   331	
   332	These bounds concern the expected operator-path norm on $E$. They do not give an
   333	$F$ estimate with constant initial-data columns. The radius substitution is
   334	numerical; cone coverage and source-to-point transfer require their separate
   335	arguments. No concentration, integration over an infinite sequence of Gaussian
   336	coordinates or nonlinear moment upper bound follows from this section alone. The
   337	constants need not be uniform as $Q,B$ tend to infinity or as model parameters
   338	approach an endpoint. For zero covariance, the operator paths and stochastic
   339	bounds vanish directly.

1	\section{Covariance bounds for physically masked wave fields}
     2	\label{S:masked-covariance}
     3	
     4	We establish the covariance estimates needed for the operator construction.
     5	Throughout this section, Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} holds, $a = \alpha_0$, and
     6	$\Gamma \ne 0$. For zero spatial covariance, the spatial spectral measures and
     7	noise variances vanish; the purely temporal estimates remain valid independently
     8	of $\Gamma$. We use the unitary Fourier transform
     9	\[
    10	  \widehat{f}(\xi) = c_d\int_{\R^d}e^{-i\xi\cdot x}f(x)\ud x,
    11	  \qquad c_d = (2\pi)^{-d/2}.
    12	\]
    13	The spectral convention in Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} means that, for every
    14	complex Schwartz test $\varphi$,
    15	\begin{equation}\label{E:masked-spectral-convention}
    16	  \int_{\R^d}\varphi(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
    17	  = \int_{\R^d}\left(\int_{\R^d}e^{i\xi\cdot x}
    18	  \varphi(x)\ud x\right)\mu(\ud\xi).
    19	\end{equation}
    20	This is an identity of distribution pairings. We will not interchange two
    21	infinite measures in the associated oscillatory expression.
    22	
    23	A positive tempered Radon measure has polynomial mass growth. Indeed, choose a
    24	nonnegative compact smooth test that is at least one on the unit ball, and apply
    25	a defining Schwartz seminorm bound for the distribution to its dilations. Its
    26	mass on a ball of radius $R \ge 1$ is bounded by a power of $R$. Summation over
    27	dyadic shells then gives integrability of $(1+|x|)^{-N}$ for some $N$, and hence
    28	absolute integrability of every Schwartz test. These facts apply to both
    29	$\Gamma$ and $\mu$. Smooth cutoffs converge in the Schwartz topology, so these
    30	integrals agree with the tempered pairings.
    31	
    32	\subsection{Translated spectral growth and physical masks}
    33	
    34	\begin{proposition}[Translated spectral mass]\label{P:masked-spectral-growth}
    35	  Put
    36	  \[
    37	    M_\Gamma = \int_{\R^d}e^{-|x|^2/4}\Gamma(\ud x),
    38	    \qquad C_\Gamma = \frac{eM_\Gamma}{(2\sqrt{\pi})^d}.
    39	  \]
    40	  Then $0 < M_\Gamma < \infty$, and for $y \in \R^d$ and $r > 0$,
    41	  \begin{align}
    42	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
    43	    &= \left(\frac{r}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^d
    44	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{-iy\cdot x}\Gamma(\ud x),
    45	    \label{E:masked-gaussian-transform}\\
    46	    0 \le \int_{\R^d}e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
    47	    &\le \frac{r^\alpha M_\Gamma}{(2\sqrt{\pi})^d},
    48	    \qquad \mu(B(y,r)) \le C_\Gamma r^\alpha.
    49	    \label{E:masked-translated-ball}
    50	  \end{align}
    51	  The ball may be open or closed.
    52	\end{proposition}
    53	
    54	\begin{proof}
    55	  Temperedness gives finiteness of $M_\Gamma$. Its positivity follows from
    56	  $\Gamma \ne 0$. To check the Fourier constant, set $J(b) = \int_\R
    57	  e^{-Ax^2}e^{ibx}\ud x$ for $A > 0$. Squaring the real Gaussian integral and
    58	  using polar coordinates gives $J(0) = \sqrt{\pi/A}$. Differentiation and
    59	  integration by parts give $J'(b) = -bJ(b)/(2A)$. Therefore, $J(b) =
    60	  \sqrt{\pi/A}e^{-b^2/(4A)}$. Taking products over the coordinates gives
    61	  \[
    62	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{i(\xi-y)\cdot x}\ud x
    63	    = \left(\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}}r\right)^d e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}.
    64	  \]
    65	  Apply~\eqref{E:masked-spectral-convention} to the single Schwartz test
    66	  $e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{-iy\cdot x}$ to obtain \eqref{E:masked-gaussian-transform}.
    67	  Its left side is nonnegative. Taking the absolute value on the right removes
    68	  the complex phase because $\Gamma$ is nonnegative. The pushforward of $\Gamma$
    69	  by $x \mapsto rx$ assigns mass $r^{\alpha-d}\Gamma(A)$ to a Borel set $A$.
    70	  Thus,
    71	  \[
    72	    \int e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}\Gamma(\ud x) = r^{\alpha-d}M_\Gamma.
    73	  \]
    74	  This proves the Gaussian bound. On either ball $B(y,r)$ the integrand
    75	  $e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}$ is at least $e^{-1}$, proving the mass bound. This proves
    76	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-spectral-growth}.
    77	\end{proof}
    78	
    79	Choose and fix a real nonzero Schwartz function $\zeta$. For $R > 0$ put
    80	$\zeta_R(x) = \zeta(x/R)$, $k_R = \widehat{\zeta_R}$ and $L =
    81	\|\widehat{\zeta}\|_1$. Then $k_R(u) = R^d\widehat{\zeta}(Ru)$ and $\|k_R\|_1 =
    82	L > 0$. Define
    83	\begin{equation}\label{E:masked-auxiliary-measure}
    84	  \nu_R(\ud\eta) = \rho_R(\eta)\ud\eta,
    85	  \qquad \rho_R(\eta) = c_d^2L\int |k_R(\xi-\eta)|\mu(\ud\xi).
    86	\end{equation}
    87	
    88	\begin{proposition}[Auxiliary mask norm]\label{P:masked-auxiliary-norm}
    89	  The measure $\nu_R$ is even, tempered and Radon, with
    90	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-auxiliary-growth}
    91	    \nu_R(B(y,r)) \le c_d^2L^2C_\Gamma r^\alpha
    92	  \end{equation}
    93	  for all $y \in \R^d$ and $r > 0$, uniformly in $R > 0$. If $H$ is a separable
    94	  complex Hilbert space and $F$ is an $H$-valued Schwartz function, then
    95	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-hilbert-fourier}
    96	    \int \|\widehat{\zeta_RF}(\xi)\|_H^2\mu(\ud\xi)
    97	    \le \int \|\widehat{F}(\eta)\|_H^2\nu_R(\ud\eta).
    98	  \end{equation}
    99	  For a real $H$, the same assertion holds after complexification.
   100	\end{proposition}
   101	
   102	\begin{proof}
   103	  Schwartz decay of $k_R$ and polynomial growth of $\mu$ show that
   104	  $\rho_R(\eta)$ is finite at every $\eta$. On compact sets of $\eta$, the
   105	  integrands have a common integrable bound. Dominated convergence therefore
   106	  makes $\rho_R$ continuous, and $\nu_R$ is Radon. Since $\zeta$ is real,
   107	  $k_R(-u) = \overline{k_R(u)}$. Evenness of $\mu$ gives evenness of $\rho_R$.
   108	  Tonelli's theorem gives
   109	  \[
   110	    \nu_R(B(y,r)) = c_d^2L\int |k_R(u)|\mu(B(y+u,r))\ud u.
   111	  \]
   112	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-spectral-growth} and $\|k_R\|_1 = L$ give
   113	  \eqref{E:masked-auxiliary-growth}. Polynomial growth on centered balls proves
   114	  temperedness by the same dyadic argument as above.
   115	
   116	  Bochner Fourier integration gives
   117	  \[
   118	    \widehat{\zeta_RF}(\xi)
   119	    = c_d\int k_R(\xi-\eta)\widehat{F}(\eta)\ud\eta.
   120	  \]
   121	  For scalar Schwartz functions this follows by Fourier inversion and absolute
   122	  integrability. It follows next for finite-rank Hilbert-valued functions. For
   123	  general $F$, take projections onto the successive spans of a countable
   124	  orthonormal basis of its separable range closure. They converge pointwise in
   125	  norm. The Schwartz bounds on $F$ dominate the Fourier integrals, proving the
   126	  identity by dominated convergence. In a finite-dimensional space the full
   127	  identity projection suffices; the zero space is immediate. The triangle
   128	  inequality and weighted Cauchy--Schwarz yield
   129	  \[
   130	    \|\widehat{\zeta_RF}(\xi)\|_H^2
   131	    \le c_d^2L\int |k_R(\xi-\eta)|\|\widehat{F}(\eta)\|_H^2\ud\eta.
   132	  \]
   133	  Integrating against $\mu$ and applying Tonelli's theorem proves
   134	  \eqref{E:masked-hilbert-fourier}. Its right side is finite by Schwartz decay
   135	  and temperedness of $\nu_R$. This proves
   136	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-auxiliary-norm}.
   137	\end{proof}

   139	\subsection{Temporal completion and the original noise}
   140	
   141	\begin{lemma}[Temporal covariance completion]\label{L:masked-time-completion}
   142	  Let $T > 0$. The form
   143	  \[
   144	    \langle f,g\rangle_a
   145	    = \int_0^T\int_0^T f(t)g(s)|t-s|^{-a}\ud t\ud s
   146	  \]
   147	  is positive semidefinite on real compact smooth tests. Its null-quotient
   148	  completion $H_a$ is separable. The inclusion of tests extends continuously
   149	  from $L^2(0,T)$, with
   150	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-time-schur}
   151	    \|f\|_a^2 \le \frac{2T^{1-a}}{1-a}\|f\|_2^2.
   152	  \end{equation}
   153	  In its complexification the norm is given by the same double integral with
   154	  $f(t)\overline{f(s)}$. In particular, bounded measurable amplitudes on a
   155	  subinterval, extended by zero, belong to this completion.
   156	\end{lemma}
   157	
   158	\begin{proof}
   159	  Write $\Gamma_E$ for Euler's Gamma function. Away from the null diagonal,
   160	  \[
   161	    |t-s|^{-a} = \frac1{\Gamma_E(a)}\int_0^\infty
   162	    \lambda^{a-1}e^{-\lambda|t-s|}\ud\lambda.
   163	  \]
   164	  This follows by substitution in the defining Gamma integral. Moreover,
   165	  \[
   166	    e^{-\lambda|t-s|}
   167	    = \int_{-\infty}^{\min(t,s)}2\lambda
   168	    e^{-\lambda(t-u)}e^{-\lambda(s-u)}\ud u.
   169	  \]
   170	  For each $\lambda > 0$ its quadratic form is an integral of a square. All
   171	  exchanges for compact smooth tests are absolutely integrable because the
   172	  kernel row integral is at most $2T^{1-a}/(1-a)$. The same bound and $2|xy| \le
   173	  |x|^2+|y|^2$ prove~\eqref{E:masked-time-schur}. A countable $L^2$-dense family
   174	  of compact smooth tests is consequently dense in $H_a$, proving separability.
   175	  The complex quadratic form is the sum of those of the real and imaginary
   176	  parts, since symmetry cancels the imaginary cross term. Thus, the same bound
   177	  holds after complexification. Smooth density in $L^2$, together with the Schur
   178	  bound on the absolute bilinear form, extends the inclusion and the integral
   179	  identity to $L^2$. This includes the stated interval amplitudes. This proves
   180	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion}.
   181	\end{proof}
   182	
   183	Let $\mathcal{D}$ consist of finite sums $F(t,x) = \sum_j\tau_j(t)f_j(x)$ with
   184	real $\tau_j \in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ and real Schwartz $f_j$. These give
   185	$H_a$-valued Schwartz functions of $x$. Let $W$ denote the original real
   186	isonormal noise in~\eqref{E:cov}.
   187	
   188	\begin{proposition}[Completion on the same noise]\label{P:masked-noise-completion}
   189	  The space $\mathcal{D}$ belongs to the original test-noise completion and
   190	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-actual-noise-norm}
   191	    \E W(F)^2 = (2\pi)^d\int
   192	    \|\widehat{F}(\xi)\|_{H_a^{\mathbb{C}}}^2\mu(\ud\xi).
   193	  \end{equation}
   194	  Define the auxiliary seminorm
   195	  \[
   196	    N_R(F)^2 = (2\pi)^d\int
   197	    \|\widehat{F}(\eta)\|_{H_a^{\mathbb{C}}}^2\nu_R(\ud\eta).
   198	  \]
   199	  Then $F \mapsto W(\zeta_RF)$ extends as a contraction from the null-quotient
   200	  completion for $N_R$ into the original $L^2(\Omega)$. The extension is
   201	  centered and jointly Gaussian. For finitely many real $F_1,\ldots,F_m \in
   202	  \mathcal{D}$, their masked covariance matrix is bounded in positive
   203	  semidefinite order by the matrix of auxiliary inner products. This gives
   204	  covariance comparison for every finite linear Gaussian image and every convex
   205	  norm power $p \ge 1$.
   206	\end{proposition}
   207	
   208	\begin{proof}
   209	  For real spatial Schwartz $f,g$, put $h(z) = \int f(y+z)g(y)\ud y$. Fourier
   210	  inversion and Parseval give
   211	  \[
   212	    h(z) = \int e^{i\xi\cdot z}\widehat{f}(\xi)
   213	    \overline{\widehat{g}(\xi)}\ud\xi.
   214	  \]
   215	  Therefore,
   216	  \[
   217	    \int e^{i\xi\cdot z}h(z)\ud z
   218	    = (2\pi)^d\widehat{f}(-\xi)\overline{\widehat{g}(-\xi)}.
   219	  \]
   220	  Apply~\eqref{E:masked-spectral-convention} to the single test $h$ and reflect
   221	  $\xi$ using evenness of $\mu$. The spatial covariance is thus
   222	  $(2\pi)^d\int\widehat{f}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{g}(\xi)}\mu(\ud\xi)$. Summing
   223	  over the finitely many temporal factors gives
   224	  \eqref{E:masked-actual-noise-norm}. Schwartz decay, temperedness and temporal
   225	  integrability justify these pairings. If $W$ is initially given only on
   226	  compact spatial tests, smooth expanding cutoffs converge in the Schwartz
   227	  topology. The spectral form is continuous in that topology, admitting
   228	  $\mathcal{D}$ in the same completion.
   229	
   230	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-auxiliary-norm}, applied with $H =
   231	  H_a^{\mathbb{C}}$, gives $\E W(\zeta_RF)^2 \le N_R(F)^2$. It annihilates
   232	  auxiliary-null tests. An auxiliary Cauchy sequence thus gives a Cauchy
   233	  sequence of noise evaluations in $L^2(\Omega)$, proving the contraction
   234	  extension and its uniqueness. Every finite linear combination of the limits is
   235	  an $L^2$ limit of centered Gaussian variables. Their variances converge, so
   236	  their characteristic functions prove that the limits remain jointly centered
   237	  Gaussian.
   238	
   239	  For the finite family let $A$ be the covariance matrix and $B$ the auxiliary
   240	  Gram matrix. Applying the norm inequality to $\sum_i b_iF_i$ gives
   241	  $b^{\mathsf{T}}Ab \le b^{\mathsf{T}}Bb$ for every real vector $b$.
   242	  Diagonalizing $B-A$ constructs a centered Gaussian vector $Z$ of that
   243	  covariance, independent of the evaluation vector $X$, on a product space. Then
   244	  $X+Z$ has covariance $B$. Conditional Jensen gives $\E\|X\|^p \le \E\|X+Z\|^p$
   245	  for every norm and $p \ge 1$. Finite Gaussian moments ensure finiteness of
   246	  both sides. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:masked-noise-completion}.
   247	\end{proof}
   248	
   249	The auxiliary completion depends on $R$ and $\zeta$. Its construction does not
   250	define multiplication by $\zeta_R$ on the original noise quotient. Nor does the
   251	finite linear Gaussian comparison assert a covariance comparison for nonlinear
   252	wave solutions. The auxiliary and original test norms need not dominate one
   253	another. No spatial representative for every auxiliary class, nonnegative
   254	physical inverse covariance for $\nu_R$, or uniform density bound in $R$ is
   255	asserted.
   256	
   257	\begin{proposition}[A physical mask need not preserve noise-null tests]
   258	  \label{P:masked-quotient-obstruction}
   259	  In the admissible case $d = 2$, $\alpha = 1$, $0 < a < 1$ and $\Gamma =
   260	  \delta_0(\ud x_1)\ud x_2$, there is a real compact smooth mask $\zeta$ such
   261	  that no finite $C$ satisfies $\E W(\zeta F)^2 \le C\E W(F)^2$ for every
   262	  compact smooth test $F$.
   263	\end{proposition}
   264	
   265	\begin{proof}
   266	  Fourier inversion on Schwartz tests gives $\mu =
   267	  (2\pi)^{-1}\ud\xi_1\delta_0(\ud\xi_2)$ in the stated spectral convention. The
   268	  measure $\Gamma$ is nonnegative, even, positive definite and tempered, with
   269	  $\Gamma(cA) = c\Gamma(A)$. It therefore satisfies Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}
   270	  with $\alpha = 1$. This is not spatial white noise in dimension two. For real
   271	  compact smooth $g$, its spatial covariance is, by ordinary Fubini,
   272	  \[
   273	    V(g) = \int_\R\left(\int_\R g(x_1,x_2)\ud x_2\right)^2\ud x_1.
   274	  \]
   275	  Choose real even $\chi \in C_c^\infty(\R)$ equal to one on $[-1,1]$ and zero
   276	  outside $[-2,2]$. For example, on $1 < r = |x| < 2$ use
   277	  \[
   278	    \chi(x) = \frac{e^{-1/(2-r)}}{e^{-1/(2-r)}+e^{-1/(r-1)}}.
   279	  \]
   280	  The endpoint exponentials vanish to every order, so the plateau pastes
   281	  smoothly. Let $I_\chi = \int(\chi')^2 > 0$ and $J_\chi = \int\chi^4 > 0$.
   282	  Positivity of $I_\chi$ follows because $\chi$ is not constant, and $J_\chi \ge
   283	  2$. Put $g(x) = \chi(x_1)\chi''(x_2)$ and $\zeta(x) = \chi(x_1)\chi(x_2)$.
   284	  Their unmasked marginal vanishes since $\int\chi'' = 0$, whereas integration
   285	  by parts gives the masked marginal $-I_\chi\chi(x_1)^2$. Thus, $V(g) = 0$ and
   286	  $V(\zeta g) = J_\chi I_\chi^2 > 0$. For a nonzero nonnegative $\tau \in
   287	  C_c^\infty(0,T)$, set $F(t,x) = \tau(t)g(x)$. The temporal factor
   288	  $\|\tau\|_a^2$ is finite and strictly positive because its nonnegative
   289	  integrand is positive on a set of positive two-dimensional measure.
   290	  Consequently, the full unmasked variance is zero and the masked variance is
   291	  positive. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:masked-quotient-obstruction}.
   292	\end{proof}
   293	
   294	\subsection{Temporal modulation and continuous wave factors}
   295	
   296	Write $\langle x\rangle = \sqrt{1+x^2}$. Let $I = [s,s+h] \subset [0,T]$, with
   297	$0 < h \le 1$. Norms below are those of the complexified temporal completion in
   298	Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion}.
   299	
   300	\begin{lemma}[Modulated amplitudes]\label{L:masked-temporal-modulation}
   301	  Let $A \in C^1(I;\mathbb{C})$, $M = \sup_I|A|$ and $D = \sup_I|A'|$. For every
   302	  real $\omega$,
   303	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-temporal-modulation}
   304	    \|1_IA(t)e^{i\omega t}\|_a^2
   305	    \le C_0(a)h^{2-a}(M+hD)^2\langle h\omega\rangle^{a-1},
   306	    \qquad C_0(a) = \frac{16}{1-a}.
   307	  \end{equation}
   308	  The bound is uniform in $T,s,h,A$ and $\omega$.
   309	\end{lemma}
   310	
   311	\begin{proof}
   312	  Put $c(v) = \int_s^{s+h-v}A(u+v)\overline{A(u)}\ud u$ for $0 \le v \le h$.
   313	  Differentiation at the moving endpoint gives
   314	  \[
   315	    c'(v) = -A(s+h)\overline{A(s+h-v)}
   316	    +\int_s^{s+h-v}A'(u+v)\overline{A(u)}\ud u.
   317	  \]
   318	  Thus, $c(h) = 0$, $|c(v)| \le hM^2$ and $|c'(v)| \le M^2+hMD$. Splitting the
   319	  covariance square into its two conjugate triangles gives
   320	  \[
   321	    \|1_IA(t)e^{i\omega t}\|_a^2
   322	    = 2\operatorname{Re}\int_0^h v^{-a}e^{i\omega v}c(v)\ud v
   323	    = 2h^{2-a}\operatorname{Re}\int_0^1 y^{-a}e^{i\omega hy}f(y)\ud y,
   324	  \]
   325	  where $f(y) = c(hy)/h$. Set $K = M+hD$. Then $f(1) = 0$ and $|f|,|f'| \le
   326	  K^2$. If $K = 0$ the assertion is immediate. If $|\omega h| \le 1$, the last
   327	  integral is at most $K^2/(1-a)$ in absolute value, and $\langle\omega
   328	  h\rangle^{a-1} \ge 2^{(a-1)/2}$. The claimed constant is sufficient in this
   329	  case.
   330	
   331	  Now suppose $k = |\omega h| > 1$. On $[0,1/k]$ the integral is at most
   332	  $K^2k^{a-1}/(1-a)$. On $[1/k,1]$, integrate the exponential by parts. The
   333	  endpoint at one vanishes, while the other endpoint contributes at most
   334	  $K^2k^{a-1}$. The derivative integral, divided by $k$, is bounded by
   335	  \[
   336	    \frac{K^2}k\left(a\int_{1/k}^1 y^{-a-1}\ud y
   337	    +\int_{1/k}^1 y^{-a}\ud y\right)
   338	    \le K^2 k^{a-1}\left(1+\frac1{1-a}\right).
   339	  \]
